Finally, in the two groups of 5, those who defeated $V$ should win against those who were defeated by $V$.

It is not difficult to see that, regardless of the results within the groups, everyone except $V$ has at least 6 losses, making $V$ the true winner.

problem: 345. A pair (of distinct) natural numbers $m$ and $n$ is called "good" if these numbers consist of the same prime factors, taken, however, in (in general) different powers (example: $90=2 \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5$ and $150=2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^{2}$), and "very good" if both the pair $m, n$ and the pair $m+1, n+1$ are "good" (example: $6=2 \cdot 3$ and $48=2^{4} \cdot 3$ - since $6+1=7$, and $48+1=49=7^{2}$). Is the number of "very good" pairs of natural numbers finite or infinite?
solution:
345. It is clear that the pair of natural numbers $n$ and $n^{2}$ is "good" for any $n>1$. On the other hand, the pair of numbers $n-1$ and $n^{2}-1=(n-1)(n+1)$ is probably "good" if the number $n+1$ is a power of two, i.e., $n+1=2^{k}$, where $k \geqslant 1$ is an integer: indeed, in this case the numbers

$$
n-1 \text { and } n^{2}-1=2^{k}(n-1)
$$

differ only in that the prime factor 2 enters the second number in a power that is $k$ higher than in the first (the number $n-1$ contains the prime factor 2, since for $n+1=2^{k}$, i.e., for $n=2^{k}-1$, the number $n-1=2^{k}-2$ is also even). From this, the infinitude of the number of "very good" pairs already follows: for example, all pairs of numbers

$$
n-1=2^{k}-2 \text { and } n^{2}-1=(n-1)(n+1)=2^{k}\left(2^{k}-2\right)
$$

where $k=1,2,3, \ldots$

problem: 69. $N$ oligarchs built a country with $N$ cities, each oligarch owns exactly one city. In addition, each oligarch built several roads between the cities: any pair of cities is connected by at most one road from each oligarch (between two cities there can be several roads belonging to different oligarchs). In total, $d$ roads were built. Some oligarchs would like to form a corporation, combining their cities and roads, so that from any city of the corporation it would be possible to reach any other city of the corporation by its roads, possibly passing through cities of other oligarchs. However, it turned out that no group of fewer than $N$ oligarchs can form a corporation! What is the largest $d$ for which this is possible?
solution:
69. Answer: the maximum number of roads is $\frac{N(N-1)(N-2)}{6}$.

Let's number the oligarchs and their cities from 1 to $N$ respectively.

Estimation. We will say that a road is liked by an oligarch if it belongs to this oligarch or one of the cities at the ends of the road belongs to this oligarch. Note that a road cannot lead out of a city belonging to the owner of that city, as in this case, the owners of the cities connected by this road can form a corporation. Therefore, any road is liked by exactly three oligarchs. We will associate each road with a triplet of oligarchs who like it.

Consider an arbitrary triplet of oligarchs $A, B$, and $C$. We will prove that this triplet is associated with no more than one road. Suppose this is not the case. The chosen triplet of oligarchs can be associated with only three roads (if such exist): the road $B C$ belonging to oligarch $A$, the road $A C$ belonging to $B$, and the road $A B$ belonging to $C$. It is easy to see that whichever two of these roads the triplet $A, B, C$ is associated with, this triplet of oligarchs can form a corporation. Therefore, each triplet of oligarchs is associated with no more than one road, i.e., there are no more than $C_{N}^{3}$ roads.

Example. Let the road between cities $i$ and $j$ belong to the oligarch numbered $k$ if and only if $k > i, k > j$.

Let's check that this example satisfies the condition of the problem. Suppose this is not the case and some group of oligarchs can form a corporation. Let $M$ be the highest number of an oligarch in this corporation. Then no road leading out of city $M$ belongs to the members of the corporation, which contradicts the fact that from this city one can reach any city of the corporation.

Note that in our example, any triplet of oligarchs $i < j < k$ is associated with the road $i j$ belonging to the oligarch $k$, i.e., there are a total of $C_{N}^{3}$ roads.

problem:
## Task A-3.5.

Let $n$ be a natural number. A sequence of $2 n$ real numbers is good if for every natural number $1 \leqslant m \leqslant 2 n$, the sum of the first $m$ or the sum of the last $m$ terms of the sequence is an integer. Determine the smallest possible number of integers in a good sequence.
solution:
## Solution.

We claim that for every $n$, the smallest possible number of integers is 2.

Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2 n}$ be a good sequence of real numbers. If $n=1$, then $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ must be integers. Now let $n>1$.

Due to the condition for $m=1$, either $x_{1}$ or $x_{2 n}$ must be an integer.

Since $x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n}$ or $x_{n+1}+\cdots+x_{2 n}$ is an integer, and their sum is also an integer, we see that both of these numbers must be integers.

Furthermore, $x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n-1}$ or $x_{n+2}+\cdots+x_{2 n}$ must be an integer. If $x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n-1}$ is an integer, since $x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n}$ is an integer, we conclude that $x_{n}$ is an integer. Similarly, if $x_{n+2}+\cdots+x_{2 n}$ is an integer, we see that $x_{n+1}$ must be an integer. Therefore, either $x_{n}$ or $x_{n+1}$ must be an integer.

This shows that at least two terms of a good sequence must be integers.

Now we prove that for every natural number $n$, there exists a good sequence of real numbers with exactly two integers.

1. If $n$ is odd, we define $x_{1}=x_{n+1}=1$ and $x_{k}=\frac{1}{2}$ for all other $k \in\{1, \ldots, 2 n\}$. 1 point

Let $1 \leqslant m \leqslant n$. For odd $m$, the sum of the first $m$ terms is $1+(m-1) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$, which is an integer. For even $m$, the sum of the last $m$ terms is $m \cdot \frac{1}{2}$, which is an integer in this case.

If $m>n$, then by the proven fact, the sum of the first or last $m-n$ terms is an integer, and since $x_{1}+\cdots+x_{2 n}$ is an integer, we see that the sum of the first or last $m$ terms must also be an integer.

2. If $n$ is even, we define the sequence $x_{1}=x_{n}=1$ and $x_{k}=\frac{1}{2}$ for all other $k \in\{1, \ldots, 2 n\}$. For $m<n$. In this case, for odd $m$, the sum of the first $m$ terms is $1+(m-1) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$, and for even $m$, the sum of the last $m$ terms is $m \cdot \frac{1}{2}$, so we see that the given sequence is good.

3. 1. $18 \star \star$ Find all positive integers $n \geqslant 3$, such that the following proposition holds:

Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ be an arithmetic sequence. If $a_{1}+2 a_{2}+\cdots+n a_{n}$ is a rational number, then at least one of $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ is a rational number.
solution:
Let the common difference of the sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ be $d$, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1}+2 a_{2}+\cdots+n a_{n} & =\sum_{k=1}^{n} k\left(a_{1}+(k-1) d\right)=a_{1} \sum_{k=1}^{n} k+d \sum_{k=1}^{n} k(k-1) \\
& =\frac{n(n+1)}{2} a_{1}+\frac{d}{3} \sum_{k=2}^{n}((k+1) k(k-1)-k(k-1)(k-2)) \\
& =\frac{n(n+1)}{2} a_{1}+\frac{(n+1) n(n-1)}{3} d \\
& -\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\left(a_{1}+\frac{2(n-1)}{3} d\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

If $3 \mid(n-1)$, then from the above equation, we know that $a_{1}+2 a_{2}+\cdots+n a_{n}=\frac{n(n+1)}{2} a \frac{2 n+1}{3}$, thus, when $a_{1}+2 a_{2}+\cdots+n a_{n}$ is a rational number, $a_{\frac{2 n+1}{3}}$ is a rational number. On the other hand, if $3 \nmid(n-1)$, let $a_{1}=\sqrt{2}, d=-\frac{3}{2(n-1)} \sqrt{2}$, then each term in the arithmetic sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}$ is an irrational number, while $a_{1}+2 a_{2}+\cdots+n a_{n}=0$ is a rational number. In summary, the set of positive integers $n$ that satisfy the condition is $\left\{n \mid n \in \mathbf{N}_{+}, n \equiv 1(\bmod 3)\right\}$.

10. A city adopts a lottery system for car license plates, with 300,000 people participating in the lottery, and 30,000 slots available each month.
(1) If those who win the lottery each month exit the lottery, and those who do not win continue to the next month's lottery with an additional 30,000 people joining each month, how long on average will it take for each person to win a slot?
(2) Under the conditions of (1), if the traffic management department can control the proportion of people who win, such that the probability of winning in the first month of each quarter is $\frac{1}{11}$, the second month is $\frac{1}{10}$, and the third month is $\frac{1}{9}$, how long on average will it take for each person to win a slot?
solution:
(1) Let $p_{i}$ be the probability that a person gets a number in the $i$-th month, then $p_{i}=\left(1-\frac{1}{10}\right)^{i-1} \cdot \frac{1}{10}=\frac{1}{10} \cdot\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{i-1}$.

Thus, $E(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} i p_{i}=\frac{1}{10} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} i\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{i-1}$,
$$
\frac{9}{10} E(X)=\frac{1}{10} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} i\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{i}=\frac{1}{10} \sum_{i=2}^{\infty}(i-1)\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{i-1}=\frac{1}{10} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}(i-1)\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{i-1},
$$

Therefore, $\frac{1}{10} E(X)=\frac{1}{10} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{i-1}=\frac{1}{10} \times \frac{1}{1-\frac{9}{10}}=1 \Rightarrow E(X)=10$.
(2) According to the problem, $P(X=1)=\frac{1}{11}, P(X=2)=\frac{10}{11} \cdot \frac{1}{10}=\frac{1}{11}$,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
P(X=3)=\frac{10}{11} \cdot \frac{9}{10} \cdot \frac{1}{9}=\frac{1}{11}, P(X=4)=\frac{10}{11} \cdot \frac{9}{10} \cdot \frac{8}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{11}=\frac{8}{11} \cdot \frac{1}{11}, \\
P(X=5)=\frac{8}{11} \cdot \frac{1}{11}, P(X=6)=\frac{8}{11} \cdot \frac{1}{11}, P(X=7)=\left(\frac{8}{11}\right)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{11}, \cdots,
\end{array}
$$

Thus, $E(X)=\frac{1+2+3}{11}+\frac{4+5+6}{11} \cdot \frac{8}{11}+\frac{7+8+9}{11} \cdot\left(\frac{8}{11}\right)^{2}+\cdots$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
=\frac{1}{11} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}(9 i-3)\left(\frac{8}{11}\right)^{i-1} \Rightarrow \frac{8}{11} E(X)=\frac{1}{11} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}(9 i-3)\left(\frac{8}{11}\right)^{i} \\
=\frac{1}{11} \sum_{i=2}^{\infty}(9 i-12)\left(\frac{8}{11}\right)^{i-1}=\frac{1}{11} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}(9 i-12)\left(\frac{8}{11}\right)^{i-1}+\frac{3}{11},
\end{array}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{11} E(X)=\frac{9}{11} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{8}{11}\right)^{i-1}-\frac{3}{11}=\frac{9}{11} \times \frac{1}{1-\frac{8}{11}}-\frac{3}{11}=\frac{30}{11} \Rightarrow E(X)=10$.

problem:

The police station is located on a straight road that is infinite in both directions. Someone stole an old police car, the maximum speed of which is $90 \%$ of the maximum speed of a new car. At some point, the police station realized what had happened and sent a police officer in a new police car in pursuit. However, the problem is that the police officer did not know when the car was stolen or in which direction along the road the thief had gone. Can the police officer catch the thief?
solution:
Let's mentally send two police assistants down both sides of the road, driving at a speed greater than that of the car thief but less than that of the police officer. Let the police officer catch up with the first assistant first, then the second, then the first again, then the second again, and so on. Clearly, at some point one of the assistants will overtake the car thief, which means that the police officer will eventually catch up with the car thief.

## Answer

He will.

problem: Exercise 6. Find the largest integer $n \geqslant 3$ for which there exists a set $\mathcal{S}$ of $n$ points in the plane with the following property: every triangle (even degenerate) whose vertices belong to $\mathcal{S}$ is isosceles but not equilateral.
solution:
Solution to Exercise 6 We say that a set $\mathcal{S}$ having the required property is cute. We will prove that any cute set contains at most 6 elements. Furthermore, we will denote by $\omega_{A, B}$ the circle centered at $A$ passing through $B$, and by $\ell_{A, B}$ the perpendicular bisector of the segment $[A B]$.

First, if $\mathcal{S}$ consists of the five vertices $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{5}$ of a regular pentagon and its center $O$, it is easily verified that $\mathcal{S}$ is cute.

Conversely, let $\mathcal{S}$ be a cute set with $n \geqslant 6$ points: we will prove that $n=6$. For any points $X, Y$, and $Z$ in $\mathcal{S}$, we know that $Z$ belongs to one of the three sets $\omega_{X, Y}, \omega_{Y, X}$, or $\ell_{X, Y}$. This observation already allows us to prove the following result.

Lemma 1. Any three points in $\mathcal{S}$ are never collinear.

problem: 14. How many four-digit numbers can be formed using the digits $1$, $9$, $8$, $8$ that leave a remainder of 8 when divided by 11?
solution:
Can form 4 numbers that leave a remainder of 8 when divided by 11
14.【Solution】Using $1, 9, 8, 8$, 12 four-digit numbers can be formed, namely $1988, 1898, 1889$, $9188, 9818, 9881, 8198, 8189, 8918, 8981, 8819, 8891$.

Subtracting 8 from them results in 1980, 1890, 1881, 9180, 9810, 9873, 8190, 8181, $8910, 8973, 8811, 8883$.

Among these, only $1980, 1881, 8910, 8811$ are divisible by 11, meaning that using $1, 9, 8, 8$, 4 four-digit numbers can be formed that leave a remainder of 8 when divided by 11, i.e., $1988, 1889, 8918, 8819$.

【Another Solution】What kind of number can be divisible by 11? A rule for determining this is: compare the sum of the digits in the odd positions with the sum of the digits in the even positions. If their difference is divisible by 11, then the given number is divisible by 11; otherwise, it is not.

Now, we need a number that leaves a remainder of 8 when divided by 11. We can consider this: such a number, when added to 3, can be divisible by 11. Therefore, we get the rule for "a number that leaves a remainder of 8 when divided by 11": add the digits in the even positions to get one sum, then add the digits in the odd positions plus 3 to get another sum. If the difference between these two sums is divisible by 11, then the number is a number that leaves a remainder of 8 when divided by 11; otherwise, it is not.

To form a four-digit number that leaves a remainder of 8 when divided by 11 using $1, 9, 8, 8$, we can divide these 4 numbers into two groups, each with 2 digits. One group will be the thousands and tens digits, with their sum denoted as $A$; the other group will be the hundreds and units digits, with their sum plus 3 denoted as $B$. We need to group them appropriately so that the difference can be divisible by 11. Now, there are only 4 ways to group them:
\begin{tabular}{lll} 
& Even & Odd \\
(1) & 1,8 & 9,8 \\
(2) & 1,9 & 8,8 \\
(3) & 9,8 & 1,8 \\
(4) & 8,8 & 1,9
\end{tabular}

After verification, the first (1) grouping method meets the requirement: $A=1+8, B=9+8+3=20, B-A=11$ is divisible by 11. However, the other three groupings do not meet the requirement.

According to the rule, if a number leaves a remainder of 8 when divided by 11, then swapping any two digits in the odd positions or any two digits in the even positions will result in a new number that also leaves a remainder of 8 when divided by 11. Thus, in the first (1) grouping, either 1 or 8 can be the thousands digit, and either 9 or 8 can be the hundreds digit. This results in 4 possible arrangements: 1988, 1889, 8918, 8819.

Answer: 4 numbers can be formed that leave a remainder of 8 when divided by 11.

Let $\frac{P_{n}}{Q_{n}}=[\underbrace{1 ; 1, \ldots, 1}_{n}]$. What are $P_{n}$ and $Q_{n}$?
solution:
Note that $\frac{P_{n+1}}{Q_{n+1}}=1+\frac{1}{1+\frac{P_{n}}{Q_{n}}}=\frac{Q_{n}}{P_{n}+Q_{n}}$, that is, $P_{n+1}=Q_{n}, Q_{n+1}=P_{n}+Q_{n}$. Therefore, $P_{n+2}=Q_{n+1}=$ $P_{n}+Q_{n}=P_{n}+P_{n+1}$. Since

$P_{1 / Q_{1}}=1, P_{2 / Q_{2}}=2$, then $P_{1}=1, P_{2}=2$, and the sequence $P_{n}$ coincides with the sequence $F_{n+1}$ of Fibonacci numbers.

## Answer

$P_{n}=F_{n+1}, Q_{n}=F_{n}$.

problem:
8 Given a positive integer $n(\geqslant 2)$, find the minimum value of $|X|$, such that for any $n$ two-element subsets $B_{1}, B_{2}, \cdots, B_{n}$ of the set $X$, there exists a subset $Y$ of $X$ satisfying:
(1) $|Y|=n$;
(2) For $i=1,2, \cdots, n$, we have $\left|Y \cap B_{i}\right| \leqslant 1$.
Here $|A|$ denotes the number of elements in the finite set $A$. (Leng Gangsong)
solution:
Solve $|X|_{\min }=2 n-1$.
(1) When $|X|=2 n-2$, it is not necessarily true that there exists a $Y$ that satisfies the conditions. In fact, let $X=\{1,2, \cdots, 2 n-2\}$, and consider a partition of $X$ as $B_{1}=\{1,2\}, B_{2}=\{3,4\}, \cdots, B_{n-1}=\{2 n-3,2 n-2\}$. Since $|Y|=n$, there must be at least two elements in $Y$ that belong to the same $B_{j}$, hence $\left|Y \cap B_{j}\right|>1$, which is a contradiction.
(2) We now prove that $|X|=2 n-1$ satisfies the condition.
Let $B=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} B_{i},|B|=2 n-1-z$, then there are $z$ elements that do not appear in any $B_{i}$, denoted as $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{z}$. If $z \geqslant n-1$, then taking $Y=\left\{a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n-1}, d\right\}, d \in B$ will suffice.
Assume $z<n-1$.
Suppose there are $t$ elements that appear exactly once in $B_{1}, B_{2}, \cdots, B_{n}$. Since $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|B_{i}\right|=2 n$, we have
$$
t+2(2 n-1-z-t) \leqslant 2 n,
$$

Thus,
$$
t \geqslant 2 n-2-2 z.
$$

Therefore, the elements that appear at least twice in $B_{1}, B_{2}, \cdots, B_{n}$ appear at most $2 n-(2 n-2-2 z)=2+2 z$ times in total.

Consider the elements $b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{t}$ that appear exactly once in $B_{1}, B_{2}, \cdots, B_{n}$. The number of $B_{j}$ that do not contain $b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{t}$ is at most $\frac{2+2 z}{2}=1+z$. Hence, at least $n-(z+1)=n-z-1$ of the $B_{j}$ contain $b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{t}$.

Without loss of generality, assume $B_{1}, B_{2}, \cdots, B_{n-1-z}$ each contain one of the elements $\tilde{b}_{1}, \widetilde{b}_{2}, \cdots, \tilde{b}_{n-1-z}$ from $b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots, b_{t}$ (if a $B_{l}(1 \leqslant l \leqslant n-1-z)$ contains multiple, choose one).

Since $2(n-1-z)+z=2 n-2-z<2 n-1$, there must be an element $d$ that does not appear in $B_{1}, B_{2}, \cdots, B_{n-1-z}$ but appears in $B_{n-z}, \cdots, B_{n}$. Let $Y=\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{z}, \widetilde{b}_{1}, \widetilde{b}_{2}, \cdots, \widetilde{b}_{n-1-z}, d\right\}$, then $Y$ satisfies the requirements.

problem: 1. (15 points) In a bookstore, there is a rule for "summing" discounts: "if different types of discounts apply to an item, they are applied sequentially one after another." For example, if two discounts A% and B% apply to an item, the first discount is applied to the original price, and the second discount is applied to the result of the first discount. Currently, two discounts are in effect in the store: "Autumn" at $25 \%$ and "Random" - a non-zero discount of a whole number of percent, determined at the moment of purchase. Someone with a loyalty card, which gives a $20 \%$ discount on all items, bought a book for 69 rubles, the original price of which was 230 rubles. What was the size of the "Random" discount?
solution:
Answer: $50 \%$.

Solution. Note that the sequence of applying discounts is irrelevant, since applying a discount of A\% is equivalent to multiplying the cost of the item by ( $1-\frac{A}{100}$ ). Let $R$ be the magnitude of the "random" discount. Then, as a result of "summing" the three discounts, we get

$$
230 \cdot\left(1-\frac{25}{100}\right) \cdot\left(1-\frac{20}{100}\right) \cdot\left(1-\frac{R}{100}\right)=69 \Longleftrightarrow R=50
$$

* Let $n$ be a given positive integer, find the number of positive integer solutions $(x, y)$ for $\frac{1}{n}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}, x \neq y$.
solution:
From the original equation, it can be seen that $x>n, y>n$. Therefore, let
$$
x=n+r, y=n+s, r \neq s .
$$

Substituting them into the original equation yields $n^{2}=r \cdot s$. The number of different divisors $r$ of $n^{2}$ is $d\left(n^{2}\right)$, and since $r \neq s$, we know $r \neq$ n. Therefore, the number of positive integer solutions $(x, y)$ of the original equation is $d\left(n^{2}\right)-1$.

problem:
Example 3 Solve the functional equation
$$
f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2 f(x) \cos y
$$
solution:
Given that the function equation involves two independent variables $x$ and $y$, let's assume one of the variables is a constant.
Let $x=0, y=t$, then (3) becomes
$$
f(t)+f(-t)=2 f(0) \cos t
$$

Let $x=\frac{\pi}{2}+t, y=\frac{\pi}{2}$, substituting into (3) we get
$$
f(\pi+t)+f(t)=0
$$

Let $x=\frac{\pi}{2}, y=\frac{\pi}{2}+t$, substituting into (3) we get
$$
f(\pi+t)+f(-t)=-2 f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \sin t,
$$

From (4), (5), and (6) we have
$$
f(t)=f(0) \cos t+f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \sin t \text {. }
$$

Let $a=f(0), b=f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right), t=x$, then $f(x)=a \cos x+b \sin x(a, b$ are constants).
Verification: $f(x+y)+f(x-y)$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
=a \cos (x+y)+b \sin (x+y)+a \cos (x-y)+b \sin (x-y) \\
=2 a \cos x \cos y+2 b \cos y \sin x \\
=2 f(x) \cos y .
\end{array}
$$

At the base of the pyramid $S A B C D$ lies a trapezoid $A B C D$ with bases $B C$ and $A D$, and $B C=2 A D$. Points $K$ and $L$ are taken on the edges $S A$ and $S B$, respectively, such that $2 S K=K A$ and $3 S L=L B$. In what ratio does the plane $K L C$ divide the edge $S D$?
solution:
## First Method.

The planes of the faces $SBC$ and $SAD$ pass through the parallel lines $BC$ and $AD$ and have a common point $S$. Therefore, they intersect along a line $l$, parallel to the bases of the trapezoid and passing through point $S$ (Fig.1). Let the line $CL$ intersect the line $l$ at point $P$, the line $PK$ intersect the line $SD$ at point $M$, and the line $AD$ at point $Q$. Denote $AD=a$. Then $BC=2a$. From the similarity of triangles $SLP$ and $BLC$, we find that

$$
SP=\frac{SL}{LB} \cdot BC=\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2a=\frac{2}{3}a
$$

and from the similarity of triangles $SKP$ and $AKQ$,

$$
AQ=\frac{AK}{KS} \cdot SP=2 \cdot \frac{2}{3}a=\frac{4}{3}a
$$

Then $QD=AQ-AD=\frac{4}{3}a-a=\frac{1}{3}a$, and from the similarity of triangles $SMP$ and $DMQ$ it follows that

$$
\frac{SM}{MD}=\frac{BP}{QD}=\frac{b^2}{\frac{2}{3}a}=2.
$$

## Second Method.

Let $M$ be the point of intersection of the cutting plane with the line $SD$ (Fig.2). Denote $V_{SABCD}=V, \frac{SM}{SD}=x$. Then

$$
\begin{gathered}
V_{SABC}=\frac{2}{3}V, V_{SADC}=\frac{1}{3}V, V_{SABD}=\frac{1}{3}V, V_{SBCD}=\frac{2}{3}V, \\
V_{SCKL}=\frac{SL}{SB} \cdot \frac{SK}{SA} \cdot \frac{SC}{SC} \cdot V_{SABC}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{1} \cdot \frac{2}{3}V, \\
V_{SCKM}=\frac{SK}{SA} \cdot \frac{SC}{SC} \cdot \frac{SM}{SD} \cdot V_{SACD}=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{1} \cdot x \cdot \frac{1}{3}V, \\
V_{SKLM}=\frac{SL}{SB} \cdot \frac{SK}{SA} \cdot \frac{SM}{SD} \cdot V_{SABD}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot x \cdot \frac{1}{3}V, \\
V_{SCLM}=\frac{SL}{SB} \cdot \frac{SC}{SC} \cdot \frac{SM}{SD} \cdot V_{SBCD}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{1} \cdot x \cdot \frac{2}{3}V.
\end{gathered}
$$

The condition for the points $K, L, C$, and $M$ to lie in the same plane is equivalent to the equality

$$
V_{SCKL}+V_{SCKM}=V_{SKLM}+V_{SCLM},
$$

From this, we find that $\frac{SM}{SD}=x=\frac{2}{3}$. Therefore, $SM:MD=2:1$.

## Answer

$2:1$

problem:
10.19 The digits $x (x \neq 0)$ and $y$ are such that for any $n \geqslant 1$, the number $x_{n}^{x x \cdots x} 6 y y \cdots y$ is a perfect square. Find all $x$ and $y$.
(18th All-Soviet Union Mathematical Olympiad, 1984)
solution:
［Solution］First, consider the case when $n=1$.
If
$$
\overline{x 6 y 4}=A^{2},
$$

then $A$ is a two-digit number with 2 or 8 as its unit digit, and the tens digit is no less than 3.
By examining $32^{2}, 38^{2}, 42^{2}, 48^{2}, 52^{2}, 58^{2}, 62^{2}, 68^{2}, 72^{2}, 78^{2}, 82^{2}, 88^{2}, 92^{2}, 98^{2}$, we find that only
$$
68^{2}=4624, \quad 98^{2}=9604
$$

have 6 as the hundreds digit.
In this case,
$x=4, y=2$, or $x=9, y=0$.
Furthermore, by
$$
\begin{array}{l}
(\underbrace{6 \cdots 6}_{n \uparrow} 8)^{2}=\underbrace{4 \cdots 4}_{n \uparrow} 6 \underbrace{2 \cdots 2}_{n \uparrow} 4 . \\
(\underbrace{2 \cdots 9}_{n \uparrow} 8)^{2}=\underbrace{9 \cdots 9}_{n \uparrow} 6 \underbrace{0 \cdots 0}_{n \uparrow} 4 \text {. } \\
\end{array}
$$

we know that the only solutions are
$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ x = 4 , } \\
{ y = 2 , }
\end{array} \quad \left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=9, \\
y=0 .
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

problem:
9.8. Given an $n \times n$ square. Initially, its cells are painted in white and black in a checkerboard pattern, with at least one of the corner cells being black. In one move, it is allowed to simultaneously repaint the four cells in some $2 \times 2$ square according to the following rule: each white cell is repainted black, each black cell is repainted green, and each green cell is repainted white. For which $n$ can one obtain a checkerboard pattern where black and white colors have swapped places after several moves?

(B. Truhin)
solution:
Answer. For all $n$ that are multiples of three.

Solution. Suppose we managed to repaint the cells as required by the conditions of the problem. We will call cells of the first type those that were initially white, and cells of the second type those that were black. Note that if a cell is repainted three times, it does not change its color in the end. Therefore, for a cell of the first type to become black, it needs to be repainted $3k+1$ times for some integer $k$ (for different cells, $k$ can be different). Thus, if $a$ is the number of cells of the first type, then the total number of repaintings of these cells is $3K+a$ for some integer $K$. For a cell of the second type to become white, it needs to be repainted $3m+2$ times. Thus, if $b$ is the number of cells of the second type, then the total number of repaintings of these cells is $3M+2b$ times.

Furthermore, in any $2 \times 2$ square, the number of cells of the first and second types is equal. Therefore, no matter how we repaint, the total number of repaintings of cells of the first and second types will be the same. Therefore, $3K+a=3M+2b$, from which $a+b=3(M-K+b)$, meaning the total number of cells $a+b$ is divisible by three. Thus, $n^2$ is a multiple of three, and therefore $n$ is a multiple of three.

It remains to show how to repaint a square with a side length that is a multiple of three. Cut it into $3 \times 3$ squares. Consider one of these squares. There are two cases - either the corner cells are white, or they are black. In the first case, repaint each of the four squares adjacent to the corners once, and in the second case, twice. It is easy to verify that with such repainting, the chessboard coloring will change to the opposite.

Remark. In the proof that $n$ is divisible by 3, we can consider not all $n^2$ cells, but $n$ cells in one horizontal or vertical row, for example, $n$ cells adjacent to the bottom side.

problem: 5. In the lottery box of Green Green Park, there are golden, silver, and colorful balls. The lottery participant can randomly draw 3 balls from the lottery box. Xiao Yangyang hopes to get 3 golden balls, Mei Yangyang hopes to get 2 golden balls and 1 silver ball, and Lan Yangyang hopes to get one of each kind of ball. Village Chief Man Yangyang says: “Only one of you three can be chosen to draw the lottery, no matter who is chosen, the probability of achieving your wish is the same.” There are at least $\qquad$ balls in the lottery box.

K1) Anaëlle has $2 n$ pieces, which are labeled $1,2,3, \ldots, 2 n$, as well as a red and a blue box. She now wants to distribute all $2 n$ pieces into the two boxes so that the pieces $k$ and $2 k$ end up in different boxes for each $k=1,2, \ldots, n$. How many ways does Anaëlle have to do this?

Answer: Anaëlle has $2^{n}$ possibilities.
solution:
Solution 1 (bijective): For every odd integer $1 \leq t<2 n$, call the set of all bricks whose labeling has the form $t \cdot 2^{k}$ the chain starting at $t$. As soon as we place a brick from a chain into a box, the box of all other bricks in this chain is uniquely determined due to the condition Since $t$ is odd, we also have that pieces in different chains can be placed independently of each other, since the condition only affects pairs of pieces that are in the same chain.

Since each tile is also in exactly one chain, it now follows that each permitted distribution of tiles has a corresponding arbitrary distribution of one representative per chain. (e.g. all tiles with odd labels). Because we have $n$ chains, the total number of possibilities is therefore $2^{n}$.

problem: In three geometric sequences, the first terms form a geometric sequence with a common ratio of $q_{3}=2$; the common ratios of the three geometric sequences form an arithmetic sequence with a difference of $d=1$; the sum of the second terms of the three geometric sequences is 24; and the sum of the first three terms of the third geometric sequence is 84. Write down these three geometric sequences.
solution:
The first terms of the sequences: $a, 2a, 4a;$ the ratios: $q, q+1, q+2$. According to the problem,

\[
\begin{gathered}
a q + 2a(q+1) + 4a(q+2) = 24 \\
4a + 4a(q+2) + 4a(q+2)^2 = 84
\end{gathered}
\]

From these equations, \(a=1, a'=\frac{192}{31}; q=2, q'=-\frac{7}{8}\). The sought sequences are thus:

$1, 2, 4, \ldots ; 2, 6, 18, \ldots ; 4, 16, 64, \ldots$

$\frac{192}{31}, -\frac{168}{31}, \frac{147}{31}, \ldots ; \frac{384}{31}, \frac{48}{31}, \frac{6}{31}, \ldots ; \frac{768}{31}, \frac{684}{31}, \frac{972}{31}, \ldots$

problem: Given more than three points in the plane, no three of which are collinear. Is there a circle that passes through at least three of the given points and does not contain any of them in its interior?
solution:
We can obtain a circle that meets the requirements in the following way. Choose any point $C$ from the given $n$ points, then find the point $D$ closest to $C$ among the other points. If there are multiple such points, let $D$ be any one of the closest points. Furthermore, consider the angle subtended by the segment $CD$ from all the other given points, and select the largest among these angles, with its vertex being $E$. If there are multiple angles that are not larger, let $E$ be the vertex of any such angle. Then the circle $k$ passing through the points $C, D, E$ meets the requirements, because on the one hand, it passes through at least the mentioned three points among the given points, and on the other hand, as we will show shortly, it does not contain any of the given points inside it.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_6bd040bc596ac2e0bd18g-1.jpg?height=434&width=423&top_left_y=474&top_left_x=840)

To prove the latter statement, we note that the angle $\angle CED$ is less than a right angle, because according to the choice of $D$, $CD \leq CE$, and thus the opposite angles in the triangle $CDE$ satisfy $\angle CED \leq \angle CDE$; moreover, since by the condition $E$ is not on the line $CD$, the circle $k$ exists. If now a point $F$ from the given points were inside $k$, then the intersection point of the line $CF$ with $k$ (different from $C$) denoted by $X$ (which is not one of the given points) would contain $F$ on the segment $CX$, and thus the angle $\angle CFD$, being an exterior angle of the triangle $FXD$, would be greater than the angle $\angle FXD = \angle CXD$, since it is equal to the sum of the angles $\angle FXD$ and $\angle FDX$. The angle $\angle CXD$ is either equal to the angle $\angle CED$ or complements it to $180^\circ$ - if $F$ and $X$ are on the side of the line $CD$ that does not contain $E$ - and in the latter case, $\angle CXD$ is an obtuse angle. Therefore, the angle $\angle CFD$ would definitely be greater than the angle $\angle CED$, which is impossible, so $k$ indeed does not contain any of the given points inside it.

Nagy Pál Géza (Nagykőrös, Arany J. g. IV. o. t.)

problem:
Example 8 Find all integers $a, b, c$, where $1<a<b<c$, such that $(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)$ is a divisor of $a b c-1$.

Translate the above text into English, please keep the original text's line breaks and format, and output the translation result directly.
solution:
To solve this problem, we first need to estimate the range of values for \( s = \frac{a b c - 1}{(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)} \left(s \in \mathbf{N}^{*}\right) \), and then check each possible case to determine the solution.

Solution: Given \( a \geqslant 2, b \geqslant 3, c \geqslant 4 \), we have:
\[
\frac{a-1}{a} = 1 - \frac{1}{a} \geqslant \frac{1}{2}, \quad \frac{b-1}{b} \geqslant \frac{2}{3}, \quad \frac{c-1}{c} \geqslant \frac{3}{4}.
\]

Thus,
\[
\frac{(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)}{a b c} \geqslant \frac{1}{4},
\]
which implies
\[
a b c \leqslant 4(a-1)(b-1)(c-1).
\]
Therefore,
\[
s = \frac{a b c - 1}{(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)} > 1.
\]
From \( a > 1 \), we get \( a \geqslant 3, b \geqslant 5, c \geqslant 7 \).
If \( b \geqslant 7 \), then \( c \geqslant 9 \), and thus
\[
\frac{(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)}{a b c} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{a}\right)\left(1 - \frac{1}{b}\right)\left(1 - \frac{1}{c}\right) \geqslant \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{6}{7} \cdot \frac{8}{9} = \frac{32}{63} > \frac{1}{2}.
\]

This contradicts (1). Therefore, we must have \( b = 5 \) and \( a = 3 \). Substituting into (1), we get \( 16(c-1) = 15c - 1 \), which simplifies to \( c = 15 \).

(3) If \( s = 3 \), then \( 3(a-1)(b-1)(c-1) = a b c - 1 \frac{1}{3} \).
This contradicts (2). Therefore, we must have \( a = 2 \).
If \( b \geqslant 5 \), then
\[
\frac{(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)}{a b c} \geqslant \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{5}{6} = \frac{1}{3},
\]
which contradicts (2). Therefore, we must have \( b = 3 \) or \( b = 4 \).
If \( b = 3 \), from (2) we get \( 6(c-1) = 6c - 1 \), which has no solution;
If \( b = 4 \), from (2) we get \( 9(c-1) = 8c - 1 \), which simplifies to \( c = 8 \).

In summary, the integer solutions \((a, b, c)\) that satisfy the conditions are \((3, 5, 15)\) and \((2, 4, 8)\).

problem: 66. In the box, there are 100 balls of different colors: 28 red balls, 20 green balls, 12 yellow balls, 20 blue balls, 10 white balls, and 10 black balls. If you randomly draw balls from the box, how many balls must you draw to ensure that you have 15 balls of the same color? $\qquad$
solution:
Answer: 75.
Solution: Considering the worst-case scenario, all 12 yellow balls, 10 white balls, and 10 black balls are taken out, along with 14 red balls, 14 green balls, and 14 blue balls, totaling 12+10+10+14+14+14=74 balls, none of which contain 15 balls of the same color. As long as one more ball is taken, this ball can only be one of red, green, or blue, and thus 15 balls of the same color will appear.

Therefore, at least 75 balls must be taken out to ensure that there are 15 balls of the same color.

problem: 10.1. Do there exist such rational non-integer numbers $x, y$ that a) both numbers $19 x+8 y$ and $8 x+3 y$ are integers?; b) both numbers $19 x^{2}+8 y^{2}$ and $8 x^{2}+3 y^{2}$ are integers?
solution: Answer: a) exist; b) do not exist. Solution. a) If we solve the system $\left\{\begin{array}{l}19 x+8 y=1 \\ 8 x+3 y=1\end{array}\right.$, we get $x=\frac{5}{7}, y=\frac{-11}{7}$ (of course, for such an example, the right-hand sides of the system can be chosen in many ways). b) Let $\left\{\begin{array}{l}19 x^{2}+8 y^{2}=m \\ 8 x^{2}+3 y^{2}=n\end{array}\right.$ (and $n$ are integers). Solving the system, we get $7 x^{2}=8 n-3 m, 7 y^{2}=8 m-19 n$, Let $k=8 n-3 m$ and assume, for the sake of contradiction, that $x=\frac{p}{q}$ is an irreducible fraction, where $q>1$. Then $7 p^{2}=k q^{2}$. If $q$ is divisible by 7, then from this $p$ must also be divisible by 7, which contradicts the irreducibility of the fraction $\frac{p}{q}$. Therefore, $k$ must be divisible by 7, i.e., $k=7 l$ (where $l$ is an integer), and thus $p^{2}=l q^{2}$, so $l$ must be a perfect square: $l=l_{1}^{2}$ (where $l_{1}$ is an integer). Therefore, $x=\frac{p}{q}=l_{1}-$ is an integer. We have reached a contradiction.

problem: 3. Is the equation $y^{2}+y=x^{3}-x$ solvable in coprime natural numbers? Answer. No.
solution:
Solution. Rewrite the equation as $y(y+1)=x\left(x^{2}-1\right)$. By the condition $\operatorname{GCD}(x ; y)=1$, it follows that $y+1=k x$ for some natural number $k$. Then $x^{2}-1=k y$. Eliminating $y$, we get $x^{2}-k^{2} x+k-1=0$. The discriminant of this quadratic equation $D=k^{4}-4 k+4$ must be a perfect square. However, $(k^{2}-1)^{2}<k^{4}-4 k+4<(k^{2})^{2}$. Therefore, $k=1$ and $x=1$. But then $y(y+1)=0$, a contradiction.

problem:
7.5. On each cell of a chessboard, there is a stack of several chips. In one move, one of the two operations is allowed:

- remove one chip from each stack in any vertical column;
- double the number of chips in each stack in any horizontal row.

Is it possible to clear the entire board of chips in some number of such operations?
solution:
Answer: Yes.

Solution. Let's record the number of chips in each cell of the board in an $8 \times 8$ table. In this case, there are two types of operations possible: subtracting one from each cell in any column; doubling any row. Our goal is to obtain a table filled with zeros.

First, we will turn all the numbers in the first column into zeros. If there are ones in the first column, we will double the numbers in the rows where the intersection with the first column contains ones, and then subtract one from all the numbers in the first column. It is clear that in this process, the "old" ones will remain in place, and each number in the first column that is different from one will decrease by one. If there are no ones in the first column from the beginning, we will subtract one from all its numbers until ones (at least one) appear, and then perform the already described operation. We will repeat this operation (doubling the rows where the intersection with the first column contains ones, and then subtracting one from each number in the first column) until all the numbers in the first column become ones. By then subtracting one from each number in the first column, we will turn them all into zeros.

Thus, we have obtained a table with zeros in the first column and natural numbers in the other columns. By turning the numbers in the 2nd, 3rd, ..., 8th columns into zeros in the described manner (while the already existing zeros will not be "spoiled"), we will obtain a table consisting entirely of zeros.

problem: 2. Pavel caught a certain number of spiders and clowns. When he counted all the legs, he got the number 176. How many spiders and how many clowns did Pavel catch, if their numbers are even and two-digit? (A spider has 8 legs, and a clown has 6 legs.)
solution: Solution. If $b$ marbles and $p$ clowns are caught, then $6 b+8 p=176$, i.e., $3 b+4 p=88$. From this, we get $p=22-\frac{3}{4} b$. For $b$ and $p$ to be two-digit numbers, it must be true that $8<\frac{3}{4} b<13$, i.e., $10<b \leq 17$, and for $p$ to be an even number, $b$ must be divisible by 8. problem: 3. Solve the system of equations $\left\{\begin{array}{l}x^{2} y-x y^{2}-5 x+5 y+3=0, \\ x^{3} y-x y^{3}-5 x^{2}+5 y^{2}+15=0 .\end{array}\right.$
solution:
Answer: $(4 ; 1)$.

Solution. The given system is equivalent to the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ x y ( x - y ) - 5 ( x - y ) + 3 = 0 } \\
{ x y ( x ^ { 2 } - y ^ { 2 } ) - 5 ( x ^ { 2 } - y ^ { 2 } ) + 1 5 = 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
((x y-5)(x-y)=-3 \\
(x y-5)(x-y)(x+y)=-15
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Dividing the second equation of the last system term by term by the first, we get $x+y=5$, from which $y=-x+5$. Substituting this into the first equation: $\left(-x^{2}+5 x-5\right)(2 x-5)=-3,2 x^{3}-15 x^{2}+35 x-28=0$. By trial, we find the integer root of this equation - $x=4$. Factoring out $(x-4)$, we get $(x-4)\left(2 x^{2}-7 x+7\right)=0$. Therefore, the equation has only one root $x=4$. Then $y=1$, and the pair of numbers $(4 ; 1)$ is the only solution to the system.

problem: 3. Circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ respectively intersect at point $B$. The extension of segment $O_{2} B$ beyond point $B$ intersects circle $\omega_{1}$ at point $K$, and the extension of segment $O_{1} B$ beyond point $B$ intersects circle $\omega_{2}$ at point $L$. The line passing through point $B$ parallel to $K L$ intersects circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ again at points $A$ and $C$ respectively. The rays $A K$ and $C L$ intersect at point $N$. Find the angle between the lines $O_{1} N$ and $O_{2} B$.
solution:
Answer: $90^{\circ}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_c43b1f7fb831d10d42ecg-23.jpg?height=483&width=662&top_left_y=267&top_left_x=731)

Solution. Since $\angle O_{1} B K = \angle O_{2} B L$, the isosceles triangles $O_{1} B K$ and $O_{2} B L$ are similar. Therefore, their vertex angles are equal. Let the common value of these angles be $2 \alpha$. Since an inscribed angle is half the corresponding central angle, we have $\angle B C L = \angle B A K = \alpha$. Since $K L \| A C$, we also get $\angle K L N = \angle L K N = \alpha$. Then,

$$
\angle L N K = 180^{\circ} - 2 \angle L K N = 180^{\circ} - 2 \alpha = 180^{\circ} - \angle B O_{1} K = 180^{\circ} - \angle L O_{1} K
$$

Therefore, the quadrilateral $L N K O_{1}$ is cyclic, from which we get

$$
\angle L O_{1} N = \angle L K N = \alpha = \frac{1}{2} \angle B O_{1} K
$$

Thus, the line $O_{1} N$ is the angle bisector of the vertex angle in the isosceles triangle $B O_{1} K$, and therefore also the altitude. Hence, the lines $O_{1} N$ and $O_{2} B$ are perpendicular.

Answer: 30.

The second player can play the following strategy: (1) if the first player plays \(2 n-1\) for \(1<=n\) \(<=9\), then he replies \(2 \mathrm{n}\) with the opposite sign; (2) if the first player plays \(2 \mathrm{n}\) for \(1<=\mathrm{n}<=9\), then he replies \(2 \mathrm{n}-1\) with the opposite sign; (3) if the first player plays 19 or 20 , then he plays the other with the same sign. This secures a score of at least 39 (from (3) ) less \(9 \times 1\) (from (1) and (2) ). So he can ensure a score of at least 30.

The first player can play the following strategy: (1) he opens with 1 ; (2) if the second player plays \(2 \mathrm{n}\) for \(1 \leq \mathrm{n}<=9\), then he replies with \(2 \mathrm{n}+1\) with the opposite sign; (3) if the second player plays \(2 n+1\) for \(1<=n<=9\), then he replies with \(2 n\) with the opposite sign; (4) if any of these replies are impossible, or if the second player plays 20 , then he replies with the highest
number available with the opposite sign. If the second player does not play 20 until the last move, then this strategy ensures a score of at most 1 (from (1) ) + \(9 \times 1\) (from (2) and (3) ) + \(20=30\). Now suppose that the second player plays \(20, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\) (where \(\left.1 \leq n \leq 9\right)\) which require a reply under (4). The reason \(a_{1}\) required a move under (4) was that \(a_{1}-1\) or \(a_{1}+1\) was the 1 st player's response to 20. Similarly, the reason \(\mathrm{a}_{2}\) required a move under (4) was that \(\mathrm{a}_{2}-\) 1 or \(\mathrm{a}_{2}+1\) was the 1 st player's response to \(\mathrm{a}_{2}\), and so on. Thus the increment to the absolute value from these moves is at most \(\left|20-a_{1}+1\right|+\left|a_{1}-a_{2}+1\right|+\ldots+\left|a_{n-1}-a_{n}+1\right|+\left|a_{n}\right|=20+n\). The increment from the moves under (2) and (3) is \((9-\mathrm{n})\) x 1 , and the increment from the move under (1) is 1 . Hence the maximum absolute value is 30 .

Since the 1 st player has a strategy to do no worse than 30 and the 2 nd player has a strategy to do no worse than 30 , these strategies must actually be optimal.

problem:
14.50*. a) Find the trilinear coordinates of the vertices of the Brocard triangle.

b) Find the trilinear coordinates of the Steiner point (see problem 19.58$).
solution:
14.50. a) From the solution of problem 19.56, it follows that the vertex $A_{1}$ of the Brocard triangle is the intersection point of the lines $C P$ and $B Q$, where $P$ and $Q$ are the first and second Brocard points. Therefore, the trilinear coordinates of point $A_{1}$ are

$$
1: \frac{c^{2}}{a b}: \frac{b^{2}}{a c}=\left(a b c: c^{3}: b^{3}\right)
$$

The barycentric coordinates of this point are ( $a^{2}: c^{2}: b^{2}$ ).
b) It is more convenient to perform the calculations in barycentric coordinates. In barycentric coordinates $(\alpha: \beta: \gamma)$, the line $B_{1} C_{1}$ is given by the equation

$$
0=\begin{array}{ccc}
\alpha & \beta & \gamma \\
c^{2} & b^{2} & a^{2} \\
b^{2} & a^{2} & c^{2}
\end{array}=\alpha\left(b^{2} c^{2}-a^{4}\right)+\beta\left(a^{2} b^{2}-c^{4}\right)+\gamma\left(a^{2} c^{2}-b^{4}\right)
$$

Moreover, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$. Therefore, the line passing through point $A$ parallel to the line $B_{1} C_{1}$ is given by the equation

$$
\beta\left(a^{2} b^{2}-c^{4}+a^{4}-b^{2} c^{2}\right)+\gamma\left(a^{2} c^{2}-b^{4}+a^{4}-b^{2} c^{2}\right)=0
$$

i.e., $\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) \beta\left(a^{2}-c^{2}\right)+\gamma\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)=0$. Therefore, $\beta: \gamma=$ $=\frac{1}{c^{2}-a^{2}}: \frac{1}{a^{2}-b^{2}}$. Thus, the Steiner point has barycentric coordinates $\frac{1}{b^{2}-c^{2}}: \frac{1}{c^{2}-a^{2}}: \frac{1}{a^{2}-b^{2}}$. The trilinear coordinates of the Steiner point are

$$
\frac{1}{a\left(b^{2}-c^{2}\right)}: \frac{1}{b\left(c^{2}-a^{2}\right)}: \frac{1}{c\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)}
$$

The equation is $a(1+\mathrm{i}) x^{2}+\left(1+a^{2} \mathrm{i}\right) x+a^{2}+\mathrm{i}=0$.
solution:
Analysis: Let the real root of the equation be $x_{0}$, substitute it into the original equation, and according to the necessary and sufficient conditions for the equality of complex numbers, transform it into a real number problem to solve.

Solution: Let the real root of the equation be $x_{0}$, then $a(1+\mathrm{i}) x_{0}^{2}+\left(1+a^{2} \mathrm{i}\right) x_{0}+a^{2}+\mathrm{i}=0$, that is,
$$
\left(a x_{0}^{2}+x_{0}+a^{2}\right)+\left(a x_{0}^{2}+a^{2} x_{0}+1\right) \mathrm{i}=0 .
$$

According to the necessary and sufficient conditions for the equality of complex numbers, we get $\left\{\begin{array}{l}a x_{0}^{2}+x_{0}+a^{2}=0 \\ a x_{0}^{2}+a^{2} x_{0}+1=0\end{array}\right.$
(2) - (1), and rearrange, we get $\left(x_{0}-1\right)\left(a^{2}-1\right)=0$. Therefore, $x_{0}=1$ or $a^{2}=1$.

When $x_{0}=1$, substituting it into (1), we have $a^{2}+a+1=0$,
Clearly, this equation has no real roots, which contradicts $a \in \mathbf{R}$. Hence, $x_{0} \neq 1$.
When $a^{2}=1$, we have $a= \pm 1$. Similarly, $a=1$ is also not suitable. Therefore, $a=-1$, at this time $x_{0}=\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$.

problem: 1. Problem: $A B C D$ is a rectangle with side lengths $A B=C D=1$ and $B C=D A=2$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $A D$. Point $P$ lies on the opposite side of line $M B$ to $A$, such that triangle $M B P$ is equilateral. Find the value of $\angle P C B$.
solution:
Solution: (Kevin Shen)
$M$ is the midpoint of $A D$, by symmetry $M B=M C$. The side lengths of an equilateral triangle are all equal, so $M B=M P$.
As $M B=M C=M P, M$ is the circumcenter of triangle $B C P$. For any chord of any circle, the angle subtended at the center is always double the angle subtended at the circumference. Since $\angle P C B$ and $\angle P M B$ are both subtended by arc $B P$, we get
$$
\angle P C B=\frac{1}{2} \angle P M B=\frac{1}{2} 60^{\circ}=30^{\circ}
$$
as required.

problem: Exercise 1. Martin and Théo are playing a game: Martin writes an integer on the board. Théo then has the right to erase the number and add 2, or to erase the number and subtract 3, as many times as he wants. Théo wins if he manages to get 2020 after a finite number of steps, otherwise Martin wins. Which player has a winning strategy?
solution:
Solution to Exercise 1 We start by testing the statement for integers close to 2020. For example, we notice that if Martin writes the integers 2018, 2016, ..., Théo can write 2020 on the board by adding a sufficiently large number of 2s to the number written by Martin. We also notice that if Martin writes 2019, Théo can also win by replacing 2019 with 2021, then 2023, and finally 2023 with 2020.

This observation allows us to conjecture, on the one hand, that Théo can always win regardless of the number written by Martin, and on the other hand, that if a number \( k \) is written on the board, Théo can write the numbers \( k+1 \) or \( k-1 \) after a finite number of operations.

We will now show that Théo can always win regardless of the number written by Martin. Suppose that at a given moment, the number \( k \) is written on the board. Then, by replacing \( k \) with \( k+2 \) by adding 2, \( k+2 \) with \( k+4 \) by adding 2, and finally \( k+4 \) with \( k+1 \) by subtracting 3, Théo has replaced the number \( k \) with the number \( k+1 \) in a finite number of operations. We will call this transformation Operation A. On the other hand, if the integer \( k \) is written on the board at a given moment, by replacing \( k \) with \( k+2 \) and \( k+2 \) with \( k-1 \), Théo has replaced the integer \( k \) with the integer \( k-1 \). We will call this transformation Operation B.

Now suppose that Martin has written the number \( k_0 \) on the board. If \( k_0 = 2020 \), Théo has already won. If \( k_0 < 2020 \), by performing \( 2020 - k_0 \) times Operation A, Théo can replace the integer \( k_0 \) with 2020. If \( k_0 > 2020 \), by performing \( k_0 - 2020 \) times Operation B, Théo can again replace the integer \( k_0 \) with 2020. In all cases, Théo wins!

problem: Task 5. (20 points) A lot consisting of three packages of shares from oil extraction companies, Razneft, Dvaneft, and Trineft, is up for auction. The total number of shares in the packages of Razneft and Dvaneft is equal to the number of shares in the Trineft package. The package of Dvaneft shares is 4 times cheaper than the package of Razneft shares, and their combined value is equal to the value of the Trineft package. The price of one share of Razneft exceeds the price of one share of Dvaneft by an amount ranging from 16 thousand rubles to 20 thousand rubles, while the price of one share of Trineft fluctuates between 42 thousand rubles and 60 thousand rubles. Determine the smallest and largest percentage of the total number of shares in the lot that the Dvaneft share package can constitute.
solution:
# Solution.

Let's introduce the following notations:

$x$ - the price of one share of Dvanefte,

$y$ - the price of one share of Raznefte,

$z$ - the price of one share of Trinefte,

$n$ - the number of shares in a Dvanefte package,

$m$ - the number of shares in a Raznefte package.

The other conditions of the problem can be written as a system of equations and inequalities:
$\left\{\begin{array}{l}4 x n=y m, \\ x n+y m=z(m+n), \\ 16 \leq y-x \leq 20, \\ 42 \leq z \leq 60 ;\end{array}\left\{\begin{array}{l}\frac{m}{n}=\frac{4 x}{y}, \\ y=x+a, \\ z=x+\frac{a m}{n+m}, \\ 16 \leq a \leq 20, \\ 42 \leq z \leq 60,\end{array}\right.\right.$

We need to find the limits of the value $\frac{n}{n+m+(n+m)} \cdot 100 \%=\frac{n}{2(n+m)} 100 \%$.

If we can find the ratio $\frac{m}{n}$, the problem will be solved, since $\frac{2(n+m)}{n}=2\left(1+\frac{m}{n}\right)$.

First, let's determine under what conditions the percentage of Raznefte shares in the total lot will be the smallest. For this, $\frac{n}{2(n+m)} \rightarrow \min$, if $n \rightarrow \min , m \rightarrow \max , y-x \rightarrow \min$, therefore, $y-x=16, a=16$. If $n \rightarrow \min , m \rightarrow \max$, then $z=x+\frac{16 m}{n+m} \rightarrow \max$, therefore, $z=60$.

Then, $\frac{m}{n}=\frac{4 x}{x+16}, x=\frac{16 m}{4 n-m}, z=\frac{16 m}{4 n-m}+\frac{16 m}{n+m}=60$.

$16 m(m+n)+16 m(4 n-m)=60(4 n-m)(n+m), 80 m n=60\left(4 n^{2}+3 m n-m^{2}\right), 3 m^{2}-5 m n-12 n^{2}=0$, $3\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)^{2}-5 \frac{m}{n}-12=0, \frac{m}{n}=3, \frac{m}{n}=-\frac{4}{3}$.

According to the problem's conditions, we choose $m=3 n$, then the smallest percentage $\frac{n}{2(n+m)} 100 \%=12.5 \%$.

Similarly, let's find the largest percentage:

For this, $\frac{n}{2(n+m)} \rightarrow \max$, if $n \rightarrow \max , m \rightarrow \min , y-x \rightarrow \max$, therefore, $y-x=20, a=20$.

If $n \rightarrow \max , m \rightarrow \min$, then $z=x+\frac{20 m}{n+m} \rightarrow \min$, therefore, $z=42$.

Then, $x=\frac{20 m}{4 n-m}, z=\frac{20 m}{4 n-m}+\frac{20 m}{n+m}=42$,

$21 m^{2}-13 m n-84 n^{2}=0$

$21\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)^{2}-13 \frac{m}{n}-84=0, \frac{m}{n}=\frac{7}{3}, \frac{m}{n}=-\frac{12}{7}$.

According to the problem's conditions, we choose $m=\frac{7 n}{3}$, the largest percentage $\frac{n}{2(n+m)} 100 \%=15 \%$.

Answer. The lot contains from $12.5 \%$ to $15 \%$ of Dvanefte shares from their total number.

problem: We say that a number is ascending if each of its digits is greater than the digit to its left. For example, 2568 is ascending and 175 is not. How many ascending numbers are there between 400 and 600?
solution:
The numbers we are looking for are greater than 400 and less than 600, so the hundreds digit can only be 4 or 5. Since they are ascending numbers, the tens digit is less than the units digit. Let's see how to choose the tens and units digits.

$$
\begin{gathered}
4\left\{\begin{array}{l}
56 \\
57 \\
58 \\
59
\end{array} \quad ; 4\left\{\begin{array}{l}
67 \\
68 \\
69
\end{array} \quad ; 4\left\{\begin{array}{l}
78 \\
79
\end{array} ; 4\{89\right.\right.\right. \\
5\left\{\begin{array}{l}
67 \\
68 \\
69
\end{array} \quad ; \quad 5\left\{\begin{array}{l}
78 \\
79
\end{array} ; 5\{89\right.\right.
\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore, we have 10 ascending numbers with the hundreds digit equal to 4 and six ascending numbers with the hundreds digit equal to 5. Thus, we have 16 ascending numbers between 400 and 600.

Question 4. Given a positive integer $n \geq 3$. The set $A=\left\{\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \mid x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in\{1,2, \ldots, 6063\}\right\}$. Determine whether it is possible to partition the elements of $A$ into groups, each containing 3 elements, such that the 3 elements in each group form an equilateral triangle.
(Note: If 3 $n$-tuples have equal pairwise distances, we say they form an equilateral triangle. The distance between two $n$-tuples $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ and $\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}\right)$ is defined as $\sqrt{\left(x_{1}-y_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{2}-y_{2}\right)^{2}+\ldots+\left(x_{n}-y_{n}\right)^{2}}$. )
solution:
Answer (Proposer: Wang Zheng) The answer is no.
A point $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ is called odd (even) if $x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}$ is odd (even).
Conclusion 1. If points $X\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right), Y\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}\right), Z\left(z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots, z_{n}\right)$ form an equilateral triangle, then $X, Y, Z$ are all odd points or all even points.
Proof of Conclusion 1. Note that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-y_{i}\right)^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_{i}-z_{i}\right)^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(z_{i}-x_{i}\right)^{2}
$$

Also note that for any positive integer $k, k^{2} \equiv k(\bmod 2)$, hence
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-y_{i}\right) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_{i}-z_{i}\right) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(z_{i}-x_{i}\right)(\bmod 2),
$$

Thus
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-y_{i}\right) \equiv 3 \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-y_{i}\right) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-y_{i}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_{i}-z_{i}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(z_{i}-x_{i}\right) \equiv 0(\bmod 2),
$$

Therefore
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-y_{i}\right) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_{i}-z_{i}\right) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(z_{i}-x_{i}\right) \equiv 0(\bmod 2),
$$

So $X, Y, Z$ have the same parity.
Conclusion 2. Let $A$ have $o$ odd points and $e$ even points, then $|o-e|=1$.
Proof of Conclusion 2. Induction on $n$, clearly the proposition holds for $n=1$. Assume the proposition holds for $n-1$, we will prove it for $n$.

Let $A_{k}=\left\{\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in A \mid x_{1}=k\right\}$, and let the number of odd and even points in $A_{k}$ be $o_{k}$ and $e_{k}$ respectively. By the induction hypothesis, $\left|o_{1}-e_{1}\right|=1$, and $o_{k}-e_{k}=(-1)^{k-1}\left(o_{1}-e_{1}\right)$, thus
$$
|o-e|=\left|\sum_{k=1}^{6063}\left(o_{k}-e_{k}\right)\right|=\left|\left(o_{1}-e_{1}\right) \sum_{k=1}^{6063}(-1)^{k-1}\right|=\left|o_{1}-e_{1}\right|=1 .
$$

Hence Conclusion 2 holds.

Returning to the original problem, by contradiction, if it can be grouped, then by Conclusion 1, the number of odd points and even points are both multiples of 3. But by Conclusion 2, the number of odd points and even points differ by 1, a contradiction. Therefore, it cannot be grouped.

problem:
5. A right regular equilateral triangular prism is given, whose base has an area of $6.25 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$.

a) Calculate the surface area of the given prism.

b) Determine the ratio of the volumes of the circumscribed and inscribed cylinders of this prism. Is this ratio the same for every right regular equilateral triangular prism?
solution:
Solution. a) From $\frac{a^{2} \sqrt{3}}{4}=6.25 \sqrt{3}$ we get $a=5 \text{ cm}$.

b) The radius of the inscribed cylinder is $r=\frac{1}{3} h$, and the radius of the circumscribed cylinder is $R=\frac{2}{3} h=2 r$, where $h$ is the height of the base. The considered cylinders have the same heights, so

$$
V_{1}: V_{2}=R^{2} \pi H: r^{2} \pi H
$$

i.e.

$$
V_{1}: V_{2}=R^{2}: r^{2}=(2 r)^{2}: r^{2}=4: 1
$$

where $V_{1}$ is the volume of the circumscribed cylinder, and $V_{2}$ is the volume of the inscribed cylinder. Thus, for all such prisms, the ratio of the considered volumes is constant.

problem: Problem 1. In two tubs, there are $4 \frac{1}{6}$ and $3 \frac{1}{2}$ liters of water respectively. How much water needs to be transferred from the first tub to the second tub so that after the transfer, both tubs have the same amount of water? Explain your answer!
solution: Solution. In the first barrel, there are $\frac{25}{6}$ liters, while in the second barrel, there are $\frac{7}{2}$ liters. From the condition of the problem, we have $\frac{25}{6}-x=\frac{7}{2}+x$. We can rewrite the last equation as $2 x=\frac{25}{6}-\frac{7}{2}$, or $x=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}$. Therefore, we need to transfer $\frac{1}{3}$ liters from the first barrel to the second barrel to have the same amount of water in both barrels.

problem:
Example 3 Find all positive integers $m, n$ such that $m^{2}-n$ divides $m+n^{2}$, and $n^{2}-m$ divides $n+m^{2}$.
(2002 Asia Pacific Mathematical Olympiad)
solution:
Analysis: By symmetry, we may assume $n \geqslant m$ and estimate the rough range of $n$.
Solution: Without loss of generality, assume $n \geqslant m$, then $(m+1)^{2}-m=(m+1)+m^{2}$. Clearly, $n^{2}-m>n+m^{2}$ holds for $n>m+1$. Therefore, when $n>m+1$, there are no integers $m, n$ that satisfy the condition. We only need to consider $n=m$ and $n=m+1$.

Assume $n=m$. Then $n^{2}-n$ divides $n^{2}+n$. If $n>3$, then $n^{2}>3 n \Rightarrow 2\left(n^{2}-n\right)>n^{2}+n$, clearly $n^{2}-n$ does not divide $n^{2}+n$ for $n>3$. Therefore, $n=2$ and $n=3$ are the only possibilities, and it is easy to verify that they work.
Assume $n=m+1$. We seek $m$ such that $m^{2}-m-1$ divides $m^{2}+3 m+1$. If $m \geqslant 6$, then
$$
m(m-5)>3 \Rightarrow 2\left(m^{2}-m-1\right)>m^{2}+3 m+1 \text{. Also, } m^{2}-m-1<m^{2}+3 m+1 \text{. }
$$

So $m^{2}-m-1$ does not divide $m^{2}+3 m+1$. For $m=1,2,3,4,5$, we verify each one and find that $m=1$ or $m=2$. In summary, the solutions are $(m, n)=(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1),(3,2),(2,3)$.
/Comment: Using inequalities to narrow down the range of variable values and verifying smaller numbers one by one is a common idea and method in number theory.

problem:
$\left[\begin{array}{l}\text { Algebraic inequalities (miscellaneous) } \\ {[\quad \text { Case analysis }}}\end{array}\right]$

$x, y>0$. Let $S$ denote the smallest of the numbers $x, 1 / y, y+1 / x$. What is the maximum value that $S$ can take?
solution:
If $x \leq \sqrt{2}$, then $S \leq \sqrt{2}$. If $y \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, then $S \leq y \leq \sqrt{2}$. If $x>\sqrt{2}, y<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, then $S \leq y+\frac{1}{x}<\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}$. Therefore, $S \leq \sqrt{2}$. Equality is achieved when $x=\frac{1}{y}=\sqrt{2}$.

## Answer

$\sqrt{2}$.

problem:
3B. Determine all pairs of integers $(x, y)$ that satisfy the equation

$$
x y + 3 y = x^2 + 6 x + 12
$$
solution:
Solution. The equation can be transformed as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}
& y(x+3)=(x+3)^{2}-9+12 \\
& y(x+3)=(x+3)^{2}+3 \\
& y=x+3+\frac{3}{x+3}
\end{aligned}
$$

The fraction $\frac{3}{x+3}$ must be an integer, so for $x \neq-3$ we have the following cases

1) $x+3=-1 \Rightarrow x=-4$ and $y=-4$
2) $x+3=1 \Rightarrow x=-2$ and $y=4$
3) $x+3=3 \Rightarrow x=0$ and $y=4$
4) $x+3=-3 \Rightarrow x=-6$ and $y=-4$

Thus, the solutions to the equation are the pairs $(-4,-4),(-2,4),(0,4),(-6,-4)$.

problem: Example 4.36. Consider the trigonometric series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a^{k} \sin k x(|a|<1)$. How many times can this series be differentiated term by term?
solution:
Solution. Consider the numerical series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{s} a^{k} (s=1, 2, \ldots)$. We will investigate their absolute convergence using the D'Alembert's ratio test (Theorem 4.8):

$$
\lim _{k \rightarrow \infty} \frac{(k+1)^{s}|a|^{k+1}}{k^{s}|a|^{k}}=|a| \lim _{k \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{k+1}{k}\right)^{s}=|a|<1
$$

According to Theorem 4.28, the series can be differentiated term by term any number of times $s$.

3. The hunter cannot ensure that the distance to the rabbit will be no more than 100 after $10^{9}$ rounds.
Let $d_{n}=A_{n} B_{n}$.
If for some $n \leqslant 10^{9}$, we already have $d_{n} \geqslant 100$, then after this, the rabbit only needs to jump in the opposite direction of the line connecting it and the hunter each time.
The following assumes $d_{n}<100$.
We only need to prove: When the rabbit moves and positions itself in a certain appropriate way, and the feedback points from the positioning device are "favorable" to the rabbit, no matter what movement strategy the hunter adopts, after 200 rounds, it cannot ensure that $d_{n+200}^{2}<d_{n}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}$, i.e., there is always a possibility that $d_{n+200}^{2} \geqslant d_{n}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}$.

Assume that after the $n$-th round, the rabbit is at $A=A_{n}$, and the hunter is at $B=B_{n}$. Without loss of generality, let the hunter know the position of $A$, which makes the information provided by the positioning device before this point negligible.

Draw the ray $B A$ (when point $B$ coincides with $A$, draw any ray starting from point $A$). Suppose the next 200 feedback points from the positioning device are exactly 200 points moving forward by a distance of 1 along the ray direction from point $A$, i.e.,
$$
A_{n} P_{n+1}=P_{n+1} P_{n+2}=\cdots=P_{n+199} P_{n+200}=1 .
$$

Let $P=P_{n+200}$.
Without loss of generality, inform the hunter of the next 200 feedback points $P_{n+1}, P_{n+2}, \cdots, P_{n+200}$ in advance, which only increases the information the hunter has.

Upon seeing these 200 feedback points, the hunter will make the following decision: Clearly, with $P$ as the center and 1 as the radius, draw a circle $\Gamma_{1}$, the rabbit is inside (including the boundary) of $\Gamma_{1}$; with $A$ as the center and 200 as the radius, draw a circle $\Gamma_{2}$, the rabbit is also inside (including the boundary) of $\Gamma_{2}$. See Figure 1.

Let the circles $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ intersect at points $X$ and $Y$. Then the rabbit could be at point $X$ or $Y$, the rabbit can jump from point $A$ to point $X$ along $A X$, or from point $A$ to point $Y$ along $A Y$, each step jumping a distance of 1, both of these jumping methods and the feedback point sequence from the positioning device comply with the rules.

Suppose the hunter moves from point $B$ to point $C$ along $B P_{n+200}$, $B C=200$. Then $d_{n+200}^{2}=C X^{2}$.

Suppose the hunter moves to some point $Z$ according to any strategy, then $Z$ is to the left of point $C$. If point $Z$ is above $B C$, then $Z Y^{2} \geqslant C Y^{2}$; if point $Z$ is below $B C$, then $Z X^{2} \geqslant C X^{2}$.
In any case, regardless of how the hunter chooses his movement method, we have $d_{n+200}^{2} \geqslant C X^{2}$.
Now calculate $C X^{2}$.
By Stewart's Theorem, we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
C X^{2}=\frac{A X^{2} \cdot C P+P X^{2} \cdot A C}{A P}-A C \cdot C P \\
=\frac{200^{2} d_{n}+1^{2}\left(200-d_{n}\right)}{200}-\left(200-d_{n}\right) d_{n} \\
=d_{n}^{2}-\frac{d_{n}}{200}+1 \geqslant d_{n}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} .
\end{array}
$$

Initially, $d_{n}=0$. Therefore, after
$$
n_{0}=4 \times 10^{6}+200<10^{9}
$$

rounds, we always have $d_{n_{0}}^{2} \geqslant 10^{4}+\frac{1}{2}$, i.e., the hunter cannot ensure that $d_{n_{0}} \leqslant 100$. Thus, after $10^{9}$ rounds, the hunter cannot ensure that the distance to the rabbit is at most 100.

problem: 8-7. Petya thought of four different digits, not equal to 0. Then he formed all possible four-digit numbers from these digits without repeating any digits. The sum of all these numbers turned out to be 73326. What 4 digits did Petya think of?
solution:
Answer: $1,2,3,5$.

Solution. Let Petya have thought of the digits $a, b, c$ and $d$. In total, there will be 24 numbers composed of these digits. If we add all these numbers, each of the digits $a, b, c$ and $d$ will appear in each place value 6 times. Therefore, the sum of all 24 numbers will be equal to $6 \cdot(a+b+c+d) \cdot 1111=73326$. From this, $a+b+c+d=11$. The number 11 can be represented as the sum of four different digits in only one way: $11=1+2+3+5$. These are the digits Petya thought of.

problem: Consider $n$ boxes aligned $B_{1}, \cdots, B_{n}$, and $n$ balls distributed in the boxes. The following operations are allowed: take a ball from box $B_{1}$ and add one to $B_{2}$, or take a ball from $B_{n}$ to add it to $B_{n-1}$, or take two balls from a box $B_{i}$ for $1<i<n$ and add one to the boxes $B_{i-1}$ and $B_{i+1}$. Is it always possible to reach a configuration where each box contains only one ball?
solution:
We proceed by induction. The result is true for 1 line. Suppose the result is true for $n-1$ boxes with $n \geqslant 1$. If at some point there are no cells with two balls, then by the pigeonhole principle, the $n$ cells each contain one ball, and consequently, we are done.

By applying successive operations, from a certain point, a ball will arrive at position $n$ or 1: indeed, we can note, for example, that the sum of the squares of the positions of the $n$ balls increases, since for any integer $n: (n+1)^{2}+(n-1)^{2}=2 n^{2}+2$, but it remains bounded by $n^{3}$, so we can bring a ball to position $n$ or 1.

Without loss of generality, assume a ball is in position $n$, then the other balls in position $n$ can be moved to position $n-1$. By the induction hypothesis, there exists a sequence of operations that allows us to end up with one ball per cell on the first $n-1$ cells if we allow:

- Removing a ball from cell 1 and placing it in cell 2.
- Removing two balls from cell $1<k<n$ - 1 and placing one in cell $k-1$ and one in cell $k+1$.
- Removing a ball from cell $n-1$ and placing it in cell $n-2$.

It is just necessary to verify that the third operation is possible with $n$ boxes using the two allowed operations: indeed, we move the ball in position $n$ to position $n-1$, then we move two balls in position $n-1$: one arrives in position $n-2$, and the ball that was initially in position $n$ returns to position $n$.

Thus, by induction, it is always possible.

326. Does the equation $x^{3}+2 y^{3}=4 z^{3}$ have solutions in natural numbers
solution:
$\triangle$ Suppose the equation has solutions in natural numbers. Consider the solution $(x_{0}; y_{0}; z_{0})$ for which the value $x=x_{0}$ is minimal. Later, we will see that if this equation has a solution in natural numbers, then it has another solution; if the equation has an infinite set of solutions in natural numbers, then from its solutions, we can always select one for which the value of $x$ is minimal, since any set of natural numbers has a smallest element.

Since $(x_{0}; y_{0}; z_{0})$ is a solution to the given equation, the equality

$$
x_{0}^{3} + 2 y_{0}^{3} = 4 z_{0}^{3}
$$

holds. Since $2 y_{0}^{3}$ and $4 z_{0}^{3}$ are divisible by 2, then $x_{0}^{3}$, and hence $x_{0}$, is also divisible by 2: $x_{0} = 2 x_{1}$, where $x_{1}$ is a natural number. Then

$$
8 x_{1}^{3} + 2 y_{0}^{3} = 4 z_{0}^{3}, \quad 4 x_{1}^{3} + y_{0}^{3} = 2 z_{0}^{3}
$$

Therefore, $y_{0}$ is divisible by 2: $y_{0} = 2 y_{1}$, where $y_{1}$ is a natural number. We get:

$$
4 x_{1}^{3} + 8 y_{1}^{3} = 2 z_{0}^{3}, \quad 2 x_{1}^{3} + 4 y_{1}^{3} = z_{0}^{3}
$$

Similarly, $z_{0}$ is divisible by 2: $z_{0} = 2 z_{1}$, where $z_{1} \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $x_{1}^{3} + 2 y_{1}^{3} = 4 z_{1}^{3}$. Compare the last numerical equality with the given equation. It turns out that if $(x_{0}; y_{0}; z_{0})$ is a solution to the equation, then $(x_{1}; y_{1}; z_{1})$, i.e., the triple $\left(\frac{x_{0}}{2}; \frac{y_{0}}{2}; \frac{z_{0}}{2}\right)$, is also a solution to this equation. But this contradicts the fact that in the solution $(x_{0}; y_{0}; z_{0})$, the value $x = x_{0}$ is the smallest of all possible.

Answer: The equation does not have solutions in natural numbers.

## § 2. Convergence of Alternating Series

$1^{\circ}$. A numerical series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$ is called alternating if among its terms there are both positive and negative ones.

Theorem 10. If the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left|v_{n}\right|$ of absolute values of the terms of the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$ converges, then the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$ also converges.

$2^{\circ}$. If an alternating series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$ converges, then the positive series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left|v_{n}\right|$ may diverge. This justifies the following definition:

If, along with the convergent alternating series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left|v_{n}\right|$ also converges, then the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$ is called absolutely convergent.

If the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$ converges, but the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left|v_{n}\right|$ diverges, then the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} v_{n}$ is called conditionally convergent, or non-absolutely convergent.

$3^{\circ}$. A special case of an alternating series is the alternating series $\left(u_{n}>0\right)$:

$$

problem: Two irreducible fractions have their denominators equal to 600 and 700. Find the minimum value for the denominator of the sum of the fractions.
solution:
Suppose the fractions are a/600 and b/700. Since they are irreducible, a and 600 have no common factor greater than 1, and the same applies to b and 700.

Adding the two fractions, we get

$$
\frac{a}{600}+\frac{b}{700}=\frac{7 a+6 b}{4200}=\frac{7 a+6 b}{2^{3} \times 3 \times 5^{2} \times 7}
$$

Observe that the numerator is not divisible by 2 or 3, because a has no common factor with 6. The numerator is also not divisible by 7 because b and 7 have no common factor.

Thus, the only factor of the denominator that we can possibly simplify is $5^{2}=25$. For this, we just need to take, for example, $a=1$ and $\mathrm{b}=3$.

$$
\frac{1}{600}+\frac{3}{700}=\frac{1}{168}
$$

Therefore, the minimum denominator of the sum is 168.

## Task 1 - 310811

On a table lie three boxes. One contains two black balls, another one black and one white ball, and the third two white balls. The boxes are labeled "Two black," "Black and white," and "Two white"; however, none of these three labels is correct.

Determine whether, under these conditions, it is possible to determine the distribution of the balls by taking out a single ball, without seeing the other balls! If this is the case, then explain how it can be done!
solution:
Since none of the labels are correct, there are only two possible distributions (one can find them, for example, by starting with the only possibilities for filling the box labeled "Two black" with something other than two black balls):

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
\text { Label } & \text { Distribution 1 } & \text { Distribution 2 } \\
\text { "Two black" } & \mathrm{s}, \mathrm{w} & \mathrm{w}, \mathrm{w} \\
\text { "Black and white" } & \mathrm{w}, \mathrm{w} & \mathrm{s}, \mathrm{s} \\
\text { "Two white" } & \mathrm{s}, \mathrm{s} & \mathrm{s}, \mathrm{w}
\end{array}
$$

If one now takes a ball from the box labeled "Black and white," the color of this ball can be used to uniquely determine:

If the ball drawn is black, then Distribution 2 is present; if it is white, then Distribution 1 is present.

problem:
## Task 2.

A cut of a finite set of points in the plane is a partition of this set into disjoint subsets $A$ and $B$, for which there exists a line that does not pass through any point of the observed set, such that all points of set $A$ are on one side, and all points of set $B$ are on the other side of this line. Determine the maximum possible number of cuts of a set of $n$ points in the plane.
solution:
## Solution.

Let the number of partitions of a set of $n$ points in the plane be at most $a_{n}$.

Consider a set $\mathcal{S}$ of $n+1$ points in the plane and note one point on the convex hull of this set, call it $T$. Observe that each partition of $\mathcal{S}$ restricts to a partition of $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$ by ignoring the point $T$. Let $\{A, B\}$ and $\{C, D\}$ be two different partitions of the set $\mathcal{S}$ that restrict to the same partition of the set $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$. This means that $\{A \backslash\{T\}, B \backslash\{T\}\}=\{C \backslash\{T\}, D \backslash\{T\}\}$. Furthermore, this means that, without loss of generality, the sets $A$ and $C$ coincide, as do the sets $B$ and $D$, except for the point $T$. However, this then means that for the partition $\{A \backslash\{T\}, B \backslash\{T\}\}$ of the set $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$, we can take a line passing through the point $T$ such that all points of the set $A \backslash\{T\}$ are on one side of this line, and all points of the set $B \backslash\{T\}$ are on the other side.

Consider all lines in the plane that pass through the point $T$ and do not pass through any point of the set $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$. Two such lines can give different partitions of the set $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$ only if there is at least one point of the set $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$ between them. Therefore, the number of different partitions of the set $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$ corresponding to some line through $T$ is at most $n$, i.e., as many as there are points in the set $\mathcal{S} \backslash\{T\}$.

Finally, we see that

$$
a_{n+1} \leqslant n+a_{n} \leqslant n+(n-1)+a_{n-1} \leqslant \cdots \leqslant n+(n-1)+\cdots+2+1+a_{1}=\binom{n+1}{2}+1
$$

Thus, a set of $n$ points in the plane can have at most $\binom{n}{2}+1$ partitions. This number is achieved, for example, by a regular $n$-gon.

problem: 10. (11th "Hope Cup" Invitational Competition Question) Let the maximum value of the function $\sqrt{\tan x-1}+\sqrt{3-\tan x}$ be $M$, and the minimum value be $N$. Then what is $\frac{M}{N}$?
solution:
10. From $1 \leqslant \tan x \leqslant 3$, it is easy to know $\sqrt{\tan x-1}+\sqrt{3-\tan x} \geqslant \sqrt{2}, N=\sqrt{2}$. Let $\vec{a}=(\sqrt{\tan x-1}, \sqrt{3-\tan x}), \vec{b}=(1,1)$, we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
2 & =(\tan x-1)+(3-\tan x) \\
& =|\dot{a}|^{2} \geqslant \frac{(\dot{a} \cdot \vec{b})^{2}}{|\vec{b}|^{2}}=\frac{(\sqrt{\tan x-1}+\sqrt{3-\tan x})^{2}}{1^{2}+1^{2}}=\frac{(\sqrt{\tan x-1}+\sqrt{3-\tan x})^{2}}{2},
\end{aligned}
$$

we can know $\sqrt{\tan x-1}+\sqrt{3-\tan x} \leqslant 2$.
$M=2$, and $N=\sqrt{2}$, so $\frac{M}{N}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}$.

problem: 4. A flea jumps along the number line, and the length of each jump cannot be less than $n$. It starts its movement from the origin and wants to visit all integer points belonging to the segment $[0,2013]$ (and only them!) exactly once. For what greatest value of $n$ will it be able to do this?
solution:
Answer: $n=1006$.

Solution: For $n=1006$, a path can be constructed as follows:

$$
0 \rightarrow 1007 \rightarrow 1 \rightarrow 1008 \rightarrow \ldots \rightarrow 1005 \rightarrow 2012 \rightarrow 1006 \rightarrow 2013
$$

We will prove that $n$ cannot be greater than 1006. Indeed, suppose $n \geqslant 1007$. Then the point with coordinate 1007 can only be reached from the start of the segment (point 0). However, if the flea jumps from there to point 1007, it cannot jump back, so it must end its path at this point and will not visit other points on the segment.

problem: IMO 1999 Problem A3 Given an n x n square board, with n even. Two distinct squares of the board are said to be adjacent if they share a common side, but a square is not adjacent to itself. Find the minimum number of squares that can be marked so that every square (marked or not) is adjacent to at least one marked square.
solution: : n/2 (n/2 + 1) = n(n + 2)/4. Solution Let n = 2m. Color alternate squares black and white (like a chess board). It is sufficient to show that m(m+1)/2 white squares are necessary and sufficient to deal with all the black squares. This is almost obvious if we look at the diagonals. Look first at the odd-length white diagonals. In every other such diagonal, mark alternate squares (starting from the border each time, so that r+1 squares are marked in a diagonal length 2r+1). Now each black diagonal is adjacent to a picked white diagonal and hence each black square on it is adjacent to a marked white square. In all 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + m-1 + m + m-2 + ... + 4 + 2 = 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + m = m(m+1)/2 white squares are marked. This proves sufficiency. For necessity consider the alternate odd-length black diagonals. Rearranging, these have lengths 1, 3, 5, ... , 2m-1. A white square is only adjacent to squares in one of these alternate diagonals and is adjacent to at most 2 squares in it. So we need at least 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + m = m(m+1)/2 white squares. 40th IMO 1999 (C) John Scholes jscholes@kalva.demon.co.uk 22 Aug 1999 Last corrected/updated 19 Aug 03
