problem:
1. On some fields of a square chessboard $n \times n (n \geq 2)$, we place a piece and then move it alternately "diagonally" and "straight". "Diagonally" means to a field that shares exactly one point with the previous one. "Straight" means to an adjacent field that shares a side with the previous one. Determine all $n$ for which there exists an initial field and a sequence of moves starting "diagonally" such that the piece visits every field of the chessboard exactly once.

(Peter Novotný)
solution:
Solution. First, we will show that the problem has a solution for any even $n$. If we place the piece, for example, on any corner square of an $n \times n$ chessboard, we can traverse the entire chessboard by moving through adjacent blocks of size $2 \times n$ in the manner indicated in Fig. 1 for $n=8$. The sequence of moves here corresponds to a sequence of consecutive directed segments. This process can be analogously applied for any even $n$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_04_17_920fc1c1e4cad7bf84a2g-01.jpg?height=479&width=500&top_left_y=820&top_left_x=455)

Fig. 1

| $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  |
| $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |
|  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  |
| $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |
|  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  | $\mathrm{B}$ |  |
| $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |  | $\mathrm{A}$ |

Fig. 2

Now we will show that for no $n \geqq 3$ odd can the chessboard be traversed in the required manner. We will prove this by contradiction. Assume that for some odd $n$ there exists a sequence of moves on an $n \times n$ chessboard that satisfies the conditions of the problem. We will color all its squares in a similar manner to a standard $8 \times 8$ chessboard, with the corner squares being black (similar to Fig. 2 for $n=7$). Furthermore, we will label all black squares with the letters $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ such that no two black squares sharing exactly one corner are labeled with the same letter. If the corner (black) squares are labeled, for example, with the letter $\mathrm{A}$, it is clear that the number of $\mathrm{A}$ squares will be $n$ more than the number of $\mathrm{B}$ squares.

We will label the squares of the chessboard that the piece will traverse in the required manner as $1,2,3, \ldots, n^{2}$ and denote the $k$-th move as $k \mapsto k+1$. If the square numbered 1 is black, the black squares will be those numbered $1,2,5,6,9,10, \ldots$; each (diagonal) move $1 \mapsto 2,5 \mapsto 6,9 \mapsto 10, \ldots$ connects black squares labeled with different letters, so the total numbers of $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ squares can differ by at most 1, which contradicts the observed difference. We reach the same contradiction if the square numbered 1 is white, in which case the black squares are those numbered $3,4,7,8,11,12, \ldots$ connected by (diagonal) moves $3 \mapsto 4,7 \mapsto 8,11 \mapsto 12, \ldots$

Thus, the problem is solved, and the solutions are all even $n \geqq 2$.

problem: Determine the sequence whose terms simultaneously form an arithmetic and geometric progression.
solution:
Let the sequence be

$$
a-d, \quad a, \quad a+d
$$

If these three terms also form a geometric sequence, then simultaneously

$$
\frac{a-d}{a}=\frac{a}{a+d}
$$

or

$$
a^{2}-d^{2}=a^{2}
$$

from which

$$
d=0
$$

Thus, the only sequence that satisfies the given conditions is one where all terms are equal. In such a sequence, the ratio of any two consecutive terms is 1, and their difference is 0. (Aladár Visnya, fóreálisk. VIII. o. t. Pécs).

The problem was also solved by: Bernát Friedmann, S.-A.-Ujhely; Béla Grünhut, Pécs; János Imre, Jr., Nyíregyháza; Elemér Meitner, Budapest; Lipót Weisz, Pécs.

problem:
10.86 Try to divide the seven digits $3,4,5,6,7,8,9$ into two groups, and arrange them into a three-digit number and a four-digit number, respectively, such that the product of these two numbers is maximized. How should the groups be divided and arranged, and prove your conclusion.
(China Beijing Junior High School Grade 3 Mathematics Competition, 1981)
solution:
[Solution] When forming each number, the larger digit should be placed at the highest position. Thus, 9 and 8 should be the leading digits of the two numbers, respectively.

Now, select one digit from the remaining digits to add to 9 and 8 to form two two-digit numbers, and make their product as large as possible. Clearly, 7 and 6 should be chosen.

Since $96 \cdot 87 > 97 \cdot 86$, among the two-digit numbers formed by two digits, the product of 96 and 87 is the largest.
From this, we consider the general case:
Let $A$ and $B$ be natural numbers, with $A > B$. Now, add the digits $c$ and $d$ ($c > d$) to $A$ and $B$ to form new numbers. There are only two possible groups:
First group: $\quad \overline{A_{c}} = 10A + c, \quad \overline{B d} = 10B + d$.
Second group: $\quad \overline{A d} = 10A + d, \quad \overline{B c} = 10B + c$.
Now, compare the products of these two groups of new numbers:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \overline{A c} \cdot \overline{B d} - \overline{A d} \cdot \overline{B c} \\
= & (10A + c)(10B + d) - (10A + d)(10B + c) \\
= & 10(A d + B c - A c - B d) \\
= & 10(A - B)(d - c) < 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$$
\overline{A c} \cdot \overline{B d} < \overline{A d} \cdot \overline{B c}.
$$

From this, we know that when dividing the four digits 9, 8, 7, and 6 into two groups to form two two-digit numbers, the first group should take 9, then the second group should take 8, and the first group should take the smaller of 7 and 6, which is 6, and the second group should take 7. This way, the product of the two two-digit numbers $96 \cdot 87$ is the largest.

Similarly, for the six digits 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, and 4, divide them into two groups to form two three-digit numbers. After the first group takes 96 and the second group takes 87, the first group should take the smaller of 5 and 4, which is 4, and the second group should take 5. This way, the product of the two three-digit numbers $964 \cdot 875$ is the largest.

Finally, there is one digit 3 left. We can add another digit 0, and add 3 and 0 to 964 and 875, respectively. According to the above conclusion, the two numbers with the largest product should be $9640 \cdot 8753$. Removing the last digit 0, forming a three-digit number and a four-digit number, their product is the largest, which is 964 and 8753.

Therefore, dividing the seven digits 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 into two groups to form a three-digit number 964 and a four-digit number 8753, the product $964 \cdot 8753$ is the largest.

problem: $7 \cdot 86$ Let $S=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right)$ be a permutation of the natural numbers $1,2, \cdots, n$. $f(S)$ is defined as the minimum value of the absolute differences between every two adjacent elements in $S$. Find the maximum value of $f(S)$.
solution:
[Solution] The maximum value of $f(S)$ is $\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$. We will prove this by considering two cases.
(1) When $n=2 k$, the absolute difference between $k$ and its adjacent numbers is no greater than $k$, so $f(S) \leqslant k=\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$. On the other hand, let $S=(k+1,1, k+2,2, \cdots, 2 k, k)$, then $f(S)=k$.
(2) When $n=2 k+1$, the absolute difference between $k+1$ and its adjacent numbers is no greater than $k$, thus $f(S) \leqslant k=\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$. In the permutation $S=(k+1,1, k+2,2, \cdots, 2 k, k, 2 k+1)$, $f(S)=k$, so we still have $f(S)=k=\left[\frac{n}{2}\right]$.

problem: Problem 4. The month of May in one year had four Mondays and four Fridays. What day of the week was May 1st?

problem: 291. Find all integers $n$ for which the fraction $\frac{n-2}{n+1}$ takes integer values.
solution:
$\triangle$ To isolate the integer part of the fraction in the numerator, we add and subtract 1 (the "plus-minus" technique):

$$
\frac{n-2}{n+1}=\frac{(n+1)-1-2}{n+1}=\frac{(n+1)-3}{n+1}=1-\frac{3}{n+1}
$$

The fraction $\frac{3}{n+1}$ must be equal to an integer. Let's consider all cases.

1) Suppose $n+1=1$. Then $n=0$.
2) Suppose $n+1=-1$. Then $n=-2$.
3) When $n+1=3$, we get $n=2$.
4) When $n+1=-3$, we find that $n=-4$.

Answer: $2,0,-2,-4$

$$
I \cdot M \cdot C=I+M+C+1007 .
$$
solution:
1. $(2,2,337)$.

If $I$, $M$, and $C$ are all odd, then $I \cdot M \cdot C$ is odd while $I+M+C+1007$ is even, which is a contradiction.
Therefore, $I$, $M$, and $C$ must include an even number, and since they are all prime numbers,
according to the size relationship, we get $I=2$.
Substituting into equation (1) yields
$$
\begin{array}{l}
2 M \cdot C - M - C = 1009 \\
\Rightarrow \quad (2 M - 1)(2 C - 1) = 2019 \\
\quad = 1 \times 2019 = 3 \times 673
\end{array}
$$
$\Rightarrow$ The prime solution is $(M, C) = (2, 337)$.
Thus, $(2,2,337)$ is the required prime solution.

problem:
Find the largest value of the expression

$$
x y+x \sqrt{1-y^{2}}+y \sqrt{1-x^{2}}-\sqrt{\left(1-x^{2}\right)\left(1-y^{2}\right)}
$$
solution:
The expression is well-defined only for $|x|,|y| \leq 1$ and we can assume that $x, y \geq 0$. Let $x=\cos \alpha$ and $y=\cos \beta$ for some $0 \leq \alpha, \beta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}$. This reduces the expression to

$$
\cos \alpha \cos \beta+\cos \alpha \sin \beta+\cos \beta \sin \alpha-\sin \alpha \sin \beta=\cos (\alpha+\beta)+\sin (\alpha+\beta)=\sqrt{2} \cdot \sin \left(\alpha+\beta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
$$

which does not exceed $\sqrt{2}$. The equality holds when $\alpha+\beta+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$, for example when $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\beta=0$, i.e., $x=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ and $y=1$.

problem: 4. Natural numbers $m, n$ are such that the fraction $\frac{m}{n}$ is irreducible, while the fraction $\frac{4 m+3 n}{5 m+2 n}$ is reducible. By which natural numbers can it be reduced?
solution:
# Answer: 7

Let the numbers $4 m+3 n$ and $5 m+2 n$ have a common divisor $d>1$. Then there exist natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that the system holds:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
4 m+3 n=a d \\
5 m+2 n=b d
\end{array}\right.
$$

From this system, we can express $m$ and $n$: $7 n=d(5 a-4 b), 7 m=d(3 b-2 a)$. If 7 does not divide $d$, then $m$ and $n$ are divisible by $d>1$, which contradicts the irreducibility of the fraction $\frac{m}{n}$. Therefore, $d=7$.

problem: 11.5. On each of ten cards, a real number is written. For each non-empty set of these cards, the sum of all numbers written on the cards in this set was found. It is known that not all of the obtained sums are integers. What is the maximum possible number of integer sums that could have resulted?
solution:
Answer: 511.

Solution: It is clear that at least one of the cards has a non-integer number, otherwise the sum of the numbers in any set would be an integer. We select one of these cards and call it $a$, and the number on it $-x$. For each set $C$ that does not contain $a$ (including the empty set), we associate the set $C \cup\{a\}$. It is clear that different sets will be mapped to different sets, because if $C \cup\{a\}$ and $D \cup\{a\}$ coincide, then $C$ and $D$ coincide. Therefore, the constructed different pairs do not have common elements.

Notice that any set $C$ will end up in one of these pairs. If it does not contain $\{a\}$, it will fall into a pair by construction; if it does contain $\{a\}$, it is paired with the set from $C$ without $\{a\}$.

Thus, all sets are divided into pairs of the form ( $C, C \cup\{a\}$ ). We discard the pair ( $\varnothing, a$ ) (since neither of these sets gives an integer sum) and look at the remaining ones. The difference in the sums of the numbers on the cards in the sets of a pair differs by the number $x$, so in each pair there is no more than one integer. Since there are $\frac{2^{10}-2}{2}=2^{9}-1=511$ pairs, there are no more than 511 sets with an integer sum.

If our set contains 9 cards with 0 and one with the number $\frac{1}{2}$, then the sum of the numbers on the cards of $2^{9}-1=511$ sets will be 0, which is an integer.

The solution includes the idea of dividing sets into such pairs that no more than one set can be taken from each - 1 point.

It is proven that there will be no more than 511 integer sums - 5 points.

problem:
In a pack of construction paper, the numbers of blue and red sheets are originally in the ratio 2:7. Each day, Laura uses 1 blue sheet and 3 red sheets. One day, she uses 3 red sheets and the last blue sheet, leaving her with 15 red sheets. How many sheets of construction paper were in the pack originally?
(A) 144
(B) 252
(C) 135
(D) 270
(E) 105
solution:
Suppose that Laura uses the last blue sheet on day number $d$.

Then the total number of blue sheets with which she started was $d$.

Since she uses 3 red sheets per day and has 15 red sheets left over, then she started with $3 d+15$ red sheets.

Since the blue and red sheets were initially in the ratio $2: 7$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{3 d+15} & =\frac{2}{7} \\
7 d & =6 d+30 \\
d & =30
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, she started with 30 blue sheets and 105 red sheets, or 135 sheets of construction paper in total.

Answer: (C)

problem: 4. If for the real numbers $x$ and $y$ the equality $(x+5)^{2}+(y-12)^{2}=14^{2}$ holds, find the smallest value of the expression $x^{2}+y^{2}$ and determine for which values of $x$ and $y$ this value is achieved.
solution:
Solution. The given equation is equivalent to the equation

$$
\left(\frac{x+5}{14}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{y-12}{14}\right)^{2}=1
$$

therefore there exists $\theta \in[0,2 \pi)$ such that $\frac{x+5}{14}=\cos \theta, \frac{y-12}{14}=\sin \theta$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2}+y^{2} & =(14 \cos \theta-5)^{2}+(14 \sin \theta+12)^{2}=365+24(12 \sin \theta-5 \cos \theta) \\
& =365+364\left(\frac{12}{13} \sin \theta-\frac{5}{13} \cos \theta\right) \\
& =365+364(\cos \varphi \sin \theta-\sin \varphi \cos \theta) \\
& =365+364 \sin (\theta-\varphi) \\
& \geq 365-364=1
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\varphi$ is the smaller acute angle of the right triangle with sides 5, 12, and 13. Therefore, the minimum value of the expression $x^{2}+y^{2}$ is equal to 1 and it is achieved for $\theta-\varphi=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$, i.e., for $\theta=\frac{3 \pi}{2}+\varphi$. In this case, since $\sin \varphi=\frac{5}{13}$ and $\cos \varphi=\frac{12}{13}$, we get

$$
x=14 \cos \theta-5=14 \sin \varphi-5=\frac{5}{13}, y=14 \sin \theta+12=14(-\cos \varphi)+12=-\frac{12}{13}
$$

problem: 4. How many integer solutions $(x, y)$ does the inequality $|x|+|y| \leq n$ have?
solution:
# Solution

Graphical interpretation of the inequality - a square with sides on the lines $x+y=n$, $-x+y=n, x-y=n,-x-y=n$. The side lying on the line $x+y=n$ corresponds to $\mathrm{n}+1$ points with integer coordinates, the side lying on the line $-x+y=n$ corresponds to $\mathrm{n}+1$ points with integer coordinates, one of which belongs to the side lying on the line $x+y=n$, so we count $\mathrm{n}$ points. The next line adds another $\mathrm{n}$ points, the fourth line adds $\mathrm{n}-1$ points. Thus, there are $4 \mathrm{n}$ points on the sides of the square. On the sides of the nearest inner square - 4(n-1) points. The origin - 1 point. The total number of points is $1+4 * 1+4 * 2+\ldots .+4 * n=1+2(n+1) n$.

problem:
674. "She was a thousand one hundred years old, She went to the hundred and first grade, She carried a hundred books in her backpack This is all true, not nonsense.

When she walked down the road, Dust rising from her ten legs, A puppy always ran behind her With one tail, but a hundred legs.

She caught every sound With her ten ears, And ten tanned hands Held her backpack and the leash.

And ten dark blue eyes

Examined the world as usual...

But everything will become quite ordinary,

When you understand our story."

(A. Starikov. "Kvant", No. 8, 1978)

So, the question is: how to interpret this story?
solution:
$\triangle$ Let's start with the phrase: "And ten tanned hands held the briefcase and the leash." How can two objects - a briefcase and a leash - be held by ten hands? Apparently, "ten hands" means two hands. This is consistent with the number of legs, ears, and eyes of the extraordinary girl. Therefore, here two units form a unit of the next higher order - similar to how in the decimal system, which we use, ten units form a unit of the next higher order - a ten.

So, what about "a hundred books," "a hundred-legged puppy," "a hundred and first class," "a thousand and a hundred years"? In our decimal system, the numbers 100, 101, and 1100 mean respectively

$$
10^{2}, \quad 10^{2}+1, \quad 10^{3}+10^{2}
$$

In the problem, since two units of each order form a unit of the next higher order, the words "a hundred," "a hundred and one," and "a thousand and a hundred" mean respectively

$$
2^{2}=4, \quad 2^{2}+1=4+1=5, \quad 2^{3}+2^{2}=8+4=12 .
$$

Now everything falls into place: the girl is 12 years old, she goes to the fifth grade, she carries four books in her briefcase, and she has a four-legged puppy.

We have encountered a system of numeration in which two units form a unit of the next higher order. Such a system is called binary.

Answer: all numbers are given in the binary system of numeration.

We use the decimal positional system of numeration. Why decimal is clear from the above; the number ten is called the base of the system. It is positional because the value of each digit depends on its p o s i t i o n, its place, as, for example, in the number 11 or 111. In the Roman system of numeration, in the notation II or III, each unit represents the same number, and between the units, there is an implied addition sign - I + I or I + I + I. The Roman system of numeration is non-positional (but decimal).

In the history of humanity, in ancient and medieval times, different peoples used various systems of numeration - with bases $2,5,10,12,20$ and 60 (they are called binary, quinary, etc., respectively), positional or, much more often, non-positional.

In the decimal positional system of numeration, the notation

$$
\overline{a_{1} a_{2} a_{3} \ldots a_{n-1} a_{n}}
$$

means the sum

$$
a_{1} \cdot 10^{n-1}+a_{2} \cdot 10^{n-2}+a_{3} \cdot 10^{n-3}+\ldots+a_{n-1} \cdot 10+a_{n}
$$

where $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{n}$ are digits, i.e., integers from 0 to 9.

Now let's take any natural number $d$, greater than 1, as the base of a positional system of numeration. The digits of this system will be all integers from 0 to $d-1$. The sum

$$
a_{1} \cdot d^{n-1}+a_{2} \cdot d^{n-2}+a_{3} \cdot d^{n-3}+\ldots+a_{n-1} \cdot d+a_{n}
$$

we will briefly write as follows:

$$
\overline{a_{1} a_{2} a_{3} \ldots a_{n-1} a_{n_{d}}}
$$

and read: the number $\overline{a_{1} a_{2} a_{3} \ldots a_{n-1} a_{n}}$ with base $d$.

The simplest (and the most ancient) is the binary system of numeration, as it has only two digits - 0 and 1, which allows operations with natural numbers to be performed very quickly. It is no coincidence that binary systems are usually used in electronic computers.

How do you translate a natural number from a non-decimal system of numeration into a decimal one? We have already answered this question in practice. For example:

$$
110101_{2}=1 \cdot 2^{5}+1 \cdot 2^{4}+0 \cdot 2^{3}+1 \cdot 2^{2}+0 \cdot 2+1=32+16+4+1=53
$$

$$
2134_{8}=2 \cdot 8^{3}+1 \cdot 8^{2}+3 \cdot 8+4=2 \cdot 512+64+24+4=1116
$$

(Note that if a number is written, say, in the octal system of numeration, all digits must be less than 8.)

And how to perform the reverse translation - from the decimal system of numeration to a given non-decimal one? We will not answer this question here, as it is rarely needed. The reader can find a detailed answer to the posed question, for example, in books [3] or [27].

Finally, let's see how operations with natural numbers are performed in systems of numeration different from the decimal one. This is done in a similar way to how it is done in the decimal system. Suppose we need to add, for example, the numbers 3546 and 6345 in the septenary system. We get:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_475fdfbb473422773b9eg-140.jpg?height=149&width=130&top_left_y=725&top_left_x=969)

When adding digits, for example, in the last column, we add 6 and 5, as in the decimal system: $6+5=11$, then we mentally represent 11 as $7+4$, write the digit 4 in the same column, and instead of 7, add 1 to the previous column, i.e., to a higher order, since $11=14$. And so on.

problem:
Task A-2.3. (10 points)

Determine all natural numbers $n$ for which

$$
5^{n}+2^{n+1} 3^{n}=9^{n}+4^{n}
$$
solution:
## Solution.

The given equation can be written in the form

$$
\begin{gathered}
5^{n}=3^{2 n}-2 \cdot 3^{n} \cdot 2^{n}+2^{2 n} \\
5^{n}=\left(3^{n}-2^{n}\right)^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

The right-hand side is a perfect square, so the left-hand side must also be a perfect square.

Therefore, $n$ is an even number, $n=2 k(k \in \mathbb{N})$.

$$
\begin{gathered}
5^{k}=3^{2 k}-2^{2 k} \\
5^{k}=\left(3^{k}-2^{k}\right)\left(3^{k}+2^{k}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

The difference between the numbers $3^{k}-2^{k}$ and $3^{k}+2^{k}$ is $2^{k+1}$, so it is not possible for both numbers to be divisible by 5. 2 points Therefore, the only possibility is $3^{k}-2^{k}=1$ and $3^{k}+2^{k}=5^{k}$, hence $k=1$. 2 points

The only solution to the given equation is $n=2 k=2$.

problem: 3. Milla was writing the letters M and L in uppercase. At the end, she counted that the letter matched the previous one 59 times, and did not match 40 times. Determine the maximum number of letters M that Milla could have written, and prove that it is indeed the maximum.
solution:
Solution. Answer: 80 letters.

For each letter except the first, it is known whether it matches the previous letter or not. Therefore, Milla wrote $1+59+40=100$ letters.

Divide all the written letters into groups of consecutive identical letters. Then, groups of M (M-groups) will alternate with groups of L (L-groups). At the beginning of each group, except the first group, there is a letter that does not match the previous letter. All other letters in the groups match the previous letter. Therefore, there are a total of $1+40=41$ groups.

problem: Ada is younger than Darwyn. Max is younger than Greta. James is older than Darwyn. Max and James are the same age. Which of the five people is the oldest?
solution:
Since Ada is younger than Darwyn, Ada cannot be the oldest.

Since Max is younger than Greta, Max cannot be the oldest.

problem:
## Task B-2.4.

For real numbers $x, y$ if the equality $|x+y|+|x-y|=2$ holds, determine the maximum value of the expression $x^{2}-6 x+y^{2}$.
solution:
## Solution.

We have the following cases:

1) $x+y \geqslant 0, x-y \geqslant 0$, that is, $y \geqslant-x, y \leqslant x$. Then we have

$$
x+y+x-y=2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=1, y \geqslant-1, y \leqslant 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=1,|y| \leqslant 1
$$

In this case, the maximum value of the expression $x^{2}-6 x+y^{2}$ is the maximum value of the expression $y^{2}-5$ for $|y| \leqslant 1$, that is, on the interval $[-1,1]$. Since the quadratic function has a minimum at its vertex, the maximum can only be achieved at the endpoints of the interval $[-1,1]$. The maximum value for $y=1$ or -1 is -4.
2) $x+y \geqslant 0, x-y \leqslant 0$, that is, $x \geqslant-y, x \leqslant y$. Then we have

$$
x+y-x+y=2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad y=1,|x| \leqslant 1
$$

In this case, the maximum value of the expression $x^{2}-6 x+y^{2}$ is the maximum value of the expression $x^{2}-6 x+1$ on the interval $[-1,1]$. The maximum is achieved for $x=-1$ and is 8.
3) $x+y \leqslant 0, x-y \geqslant 0$, that is, $x \leqslant-y, x \geqslant y$. Then we have

$$
-x-y+x-y=2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad y=-1,|x| \leqslant 1
$$

In this case, the maximum value of the expression $x^{2}-6 x+y^{2}$ is the maximum value of the expression $x^{2}-6 x+1$ on the interval $[-1,1]$, which is the same as in the previous case, 8.
4) $x+y \leqslant 0, x-y \leqslant 0$, that is, $y \leqslant-x, y \geqslant x$. Then we have

$$
-x-y-x+y=2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=-1,|y| \leqslant 1
$$

In this case, the maximum value of the expression $x^{2}-6 x+y^{2}$ is the maximum value of the expression $7+y^{2}$ on the interval $[-1,1]$. Since the quadratic function has a minimum at its vertex, the maximum can only be achieved at the endpoints of the interval $[-1,1]$, so we conclude that the maximum value is achieved for $y=1$ or -1 and is 8.

We conclude that the maximum value of the given expression is 8, and it is achieved for

$$
(x, y)=(-1,1) \quad \mathrm{and} \quad(-1,-1)
$$

We get the answer to the problem: $\frac{2 a}{a}=2$

problem: 3. Let $O$ be the center of the circumscribed circle $\mathcal{K}$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. The internal angle bisector at $A$ intersects the circle $\mathcal{K}$ again at point $D$, and the internal angle bisector at $B$ intersects the circle $\mathcal{K}$ again at point $E$. Let $I$ be the center of the inscribed circle of triangle $ABC$. What is the measure of angle $\angle A C B$ if points $D, E, O$, and $I$ lie on the same circle?
solution:
II/3. Since triangle $ABC$ is acute, points $I$ and $O$ lie on the same side of line $ED$. From the condition that points $D, E, I$, and $O$ lie on the same circle, it follows that $\angle DOE = \angle DIE$. Let's denote the angles in the triangle by $\alpha, \beta$, and $\gamma$ and express the angles $\angle DOE$ and $\angle DIE$ in terms of these.

We have $\angle DOE = \angle EOC + \angle COD$. Since a central angle is twice the inscribed angle, $\angle COE = 2 \angle CBE$. Line $EB$ is the angle bisector of $\angle CBA$, so $\angle CBE = \frac{\angle CBA}{2} = \frac{\beta}{2}$. Therefore, $\angle COE = 2 \angle CBE = \beta$. Similarly, $\angle DOC = 2 \angle DAC = 2 \cdot \frac{\alpha}{2} = \alpha$, and thus $\angle DOE = \alpha + \beta$.

We also have $\angle DIE = \angle AIB = \pi - \angle BAI - \angle IBA =$

problem: Problem 2. Grandma baked 19 pancakes. The grandchildren came from school and started eating them. While the younger grandson eats 1 pancake, the older grandson eats 3 pancakes, and during this time, grandma manages to cook 2 more pancakes. solution:
Solution. In one "cycle", the grandsons eat $1+3=4$ pancakes, and the grandmother bakes 2 pancakes, which means the number of pancakes decreases by 2. There will be ( $19-11$ ) $/ 2=4$ such cycles. This means, in these 4 cycles, the younger grandson ate 4 pancakes, the older grandson ate 12 pancakes, and the grandmother baked 8 pancakes during this time. Indeed, $19+8-4-12=11$.

Answer: 12.

problem: We write a digit in each cell of a $10 \times 10$ table such that each digit appears exactly 10 times. Can we do this in such a way that at most 4 different numbers appear in each row and column?
At least how many vertices does a graph have in which there is no cycle shorter than 6 and the degree of every vertex is 3?
solution:
Solution. We will show that the graph has at least 14 vertices, and there exists a 14-vertex graph that meets the conditions.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two vertices of the graph that are connected by an edge. Then from $A$ and $B$, two more edges each must emanate. The endpoints of these edges must be different, because if any two of them coincided, there would be a 3-length cycle in the graph. Let the other two neighbors of $A$ be $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$, and the other two neighbors of $B$ be $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$. Then $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{1}$, and $B_{2}$ must each have two more neighbors, all of which must be different vertices, because if any two of them coincided, there would be a 4 or 5-length cycle in the graph, depending on whether the common neighbor is between $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$, $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$, or one is a neighbor of $A_{i}$ and the other of $B_{j}$ (Figure 1). This adds up to $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ more vertices, so the graph has at least $2 + 4 + 8 = 14$ vertices.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_1872dd6038ffb907590bg-1.jpg?height=266&width=384&top_left_y=558&top_left_x=857)

Figure 1

A good 14-vertex graph exists, as shown in Figure 2. When selecting the neighbors of the last eight vertices $\left(A_{3}, A_{4}, A_{5}, A_{6}, B_{3}, B_{4}, B_{5}, B_{6}\right)$, it is important to ensure that the neighbors of the $A_{i}$ type vertices are all of the $B_{j}$ type, and one is a neighbor of $B_{1}$ and the other of $B_{2}$, and the same applies to the $B_{i}$ type vertices.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_1872dd6038ffb907590bg-1.jpg?height=442&width=422&top_left_y=1129&top_left_x=838)

Remark. It can be shown that a 14-vertex graph that meets the conditions is unique up to isomorphism (thus, what we see in Figures 4 and 5 is essentially the same). This graph is called the Heawood graph, and its most famous construction is related to the Fano plane (about the Fano plane, see Tamás Schmidt: Geometric spaces from an algebraic perspective (KöMaL 2004/4, pp. 199-206)). The 7 points and 7 lines of the plane give the 14 vertices of the graph. Two vertices are connected by an edge if and only if one corresponds to a line and the other to a point on that line. Since there are 3 points on every line and 3 lines through every point in the plane, every vertex in the graph has degree 3. By the definition of the graph, it is bipartite (one class contains the vertices corresponding to the points of the plane, the other the vertices corresponding to the lines of the plane), so it has no odd-length cycles. There are no 4-length cycles in the graph, otherwise there would be two different points on the plane with two different connecting lines.

What is the smallest $n$ for which this is possible?
solution:
Let's show that the conditions of the problem are met if the buttons with digits 0, 1, 3, $4, 5$ remain functional. Indeed, any digit from 0 to 9 can be represented as the sum of some two "working" digits. Let the number from 1 to 99999999 that we want to obtain consist of digits $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{8}$ (some of them, including the leading ones, may be zeros). Represent each of them as the sum of two "working" digits: $a_{1} = b_{1} + c_{1}, a_{2} = b_{2} + c_{2}, \ldots, a_{8} = b_{8} + c_{8}$. Then the number composed of "working" digits $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{8}$ and the number composed of "working" digits $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{8}$ give the desired number when summed.

Suppose that the desired result can be achieved for some set of four "working" digits. Let $a$ be some odd digit. Among the numbers from 1 to 99999999, there will be one that ends in $a$ and contains "non-working" digits in its decimal representation. Then this number can be represented as the sum of two numbers, whose representations contain only "working" digits. Therefore, for each odd digit $a$, there will be such two "working" digits (possibly the same) whose sum ends in $a$. On the other hand, it is not difficult to see that among all the sums of pairs of four "working" digits, there can be no more than four odd numbers. Therefore, one of the digits $1, 3, 5, 7, 9$ will not appear at the end of such sums. Contradiction.

problem: 1. Let $D$ be the discriminant of the reduced quadratic trinomial $x^{2}+a x+b$. Find the roots of the trinomial, given that they are distinct and one of them is equal to $D$, and the other is equal to $2D$.
solution: 1. By Vieta's theorem $b=D \cdot 2D=2D^{2}, a=-(D+2D)=-3D$, i.e., the quadratic trinomial is equal to $x^{2}-3Dx+2D^{2}$. Its discriminant $D=(-3D)^{2}-4 \cdot 2D^{2}=D^{2}$, from which $D=D^{2}$, i.e., $D=0$ (in this case both roots are the same and equal to 0) or $D=1$ (in this case the roots are 1 and 2).

problem: 【Example 4】There are $n$ money boxes, each with one key, and the keys are not interchangeable. If a key is randomly placed in each box, and then all the boxes are locked. Now, you are allowed to break open one box. How many ways are there to place the keys so that once one box is broken open, all the boxes can be subsequently opened with the keys?
solution: In order to be able to successively open all the boxes with keys after breaking open one box, the key to another box $i_{1}$ must be placed in the box that is broken open, and in box $i_{1}$, the key to box $i_{2}$ must be placed, and in box $i_{2}$, the key to box $i_{3}$ must be placed, and so on, covering every box, until the key to the box $i_{n-1}$ is placed in box $i_{n-2}$, and the key to the box that was broken open, or the key to box $i_{n}$, is placed in box $i_{n-1}$. This is equivalent to a circular permutation of $1,2, \cdots, n$, because it is sufficient to arrange $i_{1}, i_{2}, \cdots, i_{n}$ in a circle in a counterclockwise direction. Conversely, for each circular permutation of $1,2, \cdots, n$, a method of placing keys that allows all boxes to be successively opened can also be corresponded. First, let the $n$ boxes be seated in order along the circle, then place the key to the box below (determined in a counterclockwise direction) in each box, thus obtaining a method of placing keys that allows all boxes to be successively opened. Therefore, the number of ways to place keys that allow all boxes to be successively opened is exactly equal to the number of circular permutations of $1,2, \cdots, n$, which is a total of $(n-1)$! ways.

problem: 1. Find the sum of all irreducible fractions with denominator 7 that lie between the natural numbers $a$ and $b, a<b$.
solution:
Solution. Let's write $a$ and $b$ in the form $\frac{7 a}{7}$ and $\frac{7 b}{7}$. All fractions with a denominator equal to 7, including $a$ and $b$, can be written as

$$
\frac{7 a}{7}, \frac{7 a+1}{7}, \frac{7 a+2}{7}, \ldots ., \frac{7 b-1}{7}, \frac{7 b}{7}
$$

Of these, only

$$
\frac{7 a}{7}, \frac{7 a+7}{7}, \frac{7 a+14}{7}, \ldots ., \frac{7 b-7}{7}, \frac{7 b}{7}
$$

are reducible. The sum of the irreducible fractions will be calculated by subtracting the sum of the numbers in sequence (2) from the sum of all fractions in sequence (1).

The sum of the numbers in sequence (1) is the sum of numbers from an arithmetic progression with the first term $\frac{7 a}{7}$ and difference $\frac{1}{7}$. The total number of terms will be determined from the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b=a+(n-1) \frac{1}{7} \\
& 7 b=7 a+n-1 \\
& n=7 b-7 a+1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the sum of the numbers in the arithmetic progression (1) is:

$$
\frac{n}{2}\left(2 a_{1}+(n-1) d\right)=\frac{7 b-7 a+1}{2}\left[2 a+(7 b-7 a+1-1) \frac{1}{7}\right]=\frac{7 b-7 a+1}{2}(a+b) .
$$

The numbers in sequence (2) are also terms of an arithmetic progression where the difference is equal to 1 and the last term is $b$, so the number of its terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b=a+(k-1) \cdot 1 \\
& k=b-a+1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, their sum is equal to

$$
\frac{b-a+1}{2}(2 a+(b-a+1-1))=\frac{b-a+1}{2}(a+b) .
$$

Finally, the desired sum is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S & =\frac{(b+a)(7 b-7 a+1)}{2}-\frac{(b+a)(b-a+1)}{2}=\frac{b+a}{2}(7 b-7 a+1-b+a-1) \\
& =\frac{b+a}{2}(6 a-6 b)=3\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Furthermore, given that no three diagonals intersect at a single point, the number of intersection points of the diagonals inside the polygon is $C_{n}^{4}$. We first find the number of regions $g(n)$ inside the $n$-sided polygon, and then we have $f(n)=g(n)+n$.

Now, remove diagonal $l_{1}$, and let $l_{1}$ intersect with other diagonals at $d_{1}$ points. The graph $K_{n}$ is reduced by $d_{1}+1$ regions. Denote the remaining graph as $G_{1}$.

In $G_{1}$, remove diagonal $l_{2}$, and let $l_{2}$ intersect with other diagonals (excluding $l_{1}$) at $d_{2}$ points in $G_{1}$. The graph $G_{1}$ is reduced by $d_{2}+1$ regions. Denote the remaining graph as $G_{2}$.

$$

problem: Example 6. Find the mathematical expectation of a random variable $X$, having an exponential distribution.
solution:
Solution. We will use formula (2.4.8) and formula (3.6.2):

$$
M(X)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x p(x) d x=\int_{-\infty}^{0} x p(x) d x+\int_{0}^{+\infty} x p(x) d x=\int_{-\infty}^{0} 0 \cdot x d x+\int_{0}^{+\infty} x \alpha e^{-\alpha x} d x
$$

$$
M(X)=\alpha \int_{0}^{+\infty} x e^{-\alpha x} d x
$$

Applying the integration by parts formula

$$
\int_{0}^{+\infty} u d v=\left.u v\right|_{0} ^{+\infty}-\int_{0}^{+\infty} v d u
$$

assuming $u=x, d v=\alpha e^{-\alpha x} d x=-d\left(e^{-\alpha x}\right)$, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \alpha \int_{0}^{+\infty} x e^{-\alpha x} d x=-\int_{0}^{+\infty} x d\left(e^{-\alpha x}\right)=-\left.x e^{-\alpha x}\right|_{0} ^{+\infty}+\int_{0}^{+\infty} e^{-\alpha x} d x= \\
& =0-\left.\frac{1}{\alpha} e^{-\alpha x}\right|_{0} ^{+\infty}=-\frac{1}{\alpha}\left(e^{-\infty}-e^{0}\right)=\frac{1}{\alpha} . \quad M(X)=\frac{1}{\alpha}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the expected value of a random variable distributed according to the exponential law is equal to the reciprocal of the parameter $\alpha$.

Example 7. Find the variance and standard deviation of a random variable that has an exponential distribution.

**Solution.** We will find the variance using formula (2.5.14)

$$
D(x)=\int_{0}^{+\infty} x^{2} p(x) d x-(M(x))^{2}
$$

Using formula (3.6.2) and the results from Example 6, we rewrite the expression for the variance as:

$$
D(x)=\int_{0}^{+\infty} x^{2} \alpha e^{-\alpha x} d x-1 / \alpha^{2}
$$

Integrating by parts twice, we get:

$$
\int_{0}^{+\infty} x^{2} \alpha e^{-\alpha x} d x=2 / \alpha^{2}
$$

Therefore,

$$
D(x)=\alpha \int_{0}^{+\infty} x^{2} e^{-\alpha x} d x-1 / \alpha^{2}=\frac{2}{\alpha^{2}}-\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}=\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}
$$

$$
D(x)=\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}
$$

To find the standard deviation, we take the square root of the variance:

$$
\sigma(x)=\sqrt{D(X)}=\frac{1}{\alpha}
$$

Remark. The expected value and the standard deviation of the exponential distribution are equal to each other (see Example 6).

problem: Find all integers $a$ and $b$ such that $3 a^{2}=b^{2}+1$.
solution:
- The first solution is to look modulo 4. Indeed, we have seen that a square can only be congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 4, and therefore $3 a^{2}$ can only be congruent to 0 or 3 modulo 4. But in the same way, $b^{2}+1$ can only be congruent to 1 or 2 modulo 4, so there cannot be equality between the two sides, and the equation has no solution.
- A shorter method is to go directly modulo 3. Indeed, the equation becomes $b^{2}+1 \equiv 0(\bmod 3)$. However, a simple check shows us that $b^{2}$ can only be 0 or 1 modulo 3, so in all cases we have $b^{2}+1 \not \equiv 0(\bmod 3)$ and the equation has no solution.

solution:
Let $S=\{a, b\}$ be a subset of $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ that is assumed to be generating, and let $x, y, z$, $t$ be integers such that $x a+y b=\left(\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right)$ and $z a+t b=\binom{0}{1}$. Then $(z y-x t) a=\binom{-t}{y}$ and $(z y-x t) b=\binom{z}{-x}$. Since we cannot have $x=y=z=t=0$ simultaneously, it follows that $z y-x t \neq 0$. Furthermore, $(z y-x t)^{2}\left(a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}\right)=x t-z y$, so $(x t-z y)\left(a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}\right)=1$. Since $x t-z y$ and $a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}$ are integers, it follows that $a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}= \pm 1$.

Conversely, if $a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}=\varepsilon \in\{-1,1\}$, then for all integers $u$ and $v,\binom{u}{v}=$ $\varepsilon\left(b_{1} v-b_{2} u\right) a+\varepsilon\left(a_{2} u-a_{1} v\right) b$.

Finally, if $a=b$, then it is clear that $a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}=0 \notin\{-1,1\}$. It follows that the generating subsets of $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ of cardinality at most 2 are the sets $\{a, b\} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^{2}$ such that $a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}= \pm 1$.

On an infinite chessboard, a closed non-self-intersecting broken line is drawn, passing along the edges of the cells. Inside the broken line, there are $k$ black cells. What is the maximum area that the figure bounded by this broken line can have?
solution:
We will gradually repaint our figure. On the first step, we will repaint one of the black cells to blue, and all its white neighbors belonging to the figure - to yellow. On the next step, we will repaint a black cell adjacent to a yellow one to blue, and all its white neighbors - to yellow. And so on.

Since the figure is connected and there are exactly $k$ black cells, it will take exactly $\mathrm{k}$ steps to repaint the entire figure. On the first step, no more than five cells are repainted, and on each of the subsequent steps - no more than four (one black and three white). Therefore, there are no more than $4 k+1$ cells in the figure.

problem: | Construct the section of the triangular prism $A B C A 1 B 1 C 1$ by a plane passing through points $A 1$ and $C$ and parallel to the line $B C 1$. In what ratio does this plane divide the edge $A B$?
solution:
The plane $B B 1 C 1$ passes through the line $B C 1$ and intersects the secant plane along the line $a$, passing through point $C$. Since the line $B C 1$ is parallel to the secant plane, $a \| B C 1$. From this, the following construction follows. Through point $C$, draw a line $a$ parallel to $B C 1$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points of intersection of this line with the extensions of the edges $B 1 C 1$ and $B 1 B$, respectively, and let $M$ be the point of intersection of $A 1 Q$ and $A B$. Then the desired section is the triangle $A 1 M C$. Since $B C$ is the midline of triangle $Q B 1 P$, the segment $B M$ is the midline of triangle $A 1 Q B 1$, therefore

$$
B M=\frac{1}{2} A 1 B 1=\frac{1}{2} A B
$$

Thus, $A M: M B=1: 1$.

## Answer

$1: 1$.

problem:
João is playing a game where the only allowed operation is to replace the natural number $n$ with the natural number $a \cdot b$ if $a+b=n$, with $a$ and $b$ being natural numbers. For example, if the last number obtained was 15, he can replace it with $56=7 \cdot 8$, since $7+8=15$ and both are natural numbers.

a) Starting with the number 7, show a sequence of operations that produces the number 48.

b) Starting with the number 7, show a sequence of operations that produces the number 2014.

#
solution:
Solution

a) Let's indicate the swap operations with an arrow $(\rightarrow)$. One way would be:

$$
7=2+5 \rightarrow 10=2+8 \rightarrow 16=12+4 \rightarrow 48
$$

b) Since $n=(n-1)+1$, it is possible to decrease $n$ by one unit, transforming it into $1 \cdot(n-1)=n-1$. Therefore, a good strategy would be to create a number larger than 2014 and then use the previous operation to decrease it by one unit at a time until we obtain the number 2014. To get a number larger than 2014, do:

$$
7=2+5 \rightarrow 10=5+5 \rightarrow 25=12+13 \rightarrow 156=100+56 \rightarrow 5600
$$

Now we just need to decrease it by one unit $5600-2014=3586$ times.

Certainly, there are faster ways that use fewer instances of the described operation. One of them would be:

$$
7=2+5 \rightarrow 10=9+1 \rightarrow 9=4+5 \rightarrow 20=7+13 \rightarrow 91=38+53 \rightarrow 2014
$$

problem:
Let $X$ be a subset of $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 10000\}$ with the following property: If $a, b \in X, a \neq b$, then $a \cdot b \notin X$. What is the maximal number of elements in $X$ ?

Answer: 9901.
solution:
If $X=\{100,101,102, \ldots, 9999,10000\}$, then for any two selected $a$ and $b, a \neq b$, $a \cdot b \geq 100 \cdot 101>10000$, so $a \cdot b \notin X$. So $X$ may have 9901 elements.

Suppose that $x_{1}1$ and consider the pairs

$$
\begin{gathered}
200-x_{1},\left(200-x_{1}\right) \cdot x_{1} \\
200-x_{2},\left(200-x_{2}\right) \cdot x_{2} \\
\vdots \\
200-x_{k},\left(200-x_{k}\right) \cdot x_{k}
\end{gathered}
$$

Clearly $x_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{k}<100<200-x_{k}<200-x_{k-1}<\cdots<200-x_{2}<$ $200-x_{1}<200<\left(200-x_{1}\right) \cdot x_{1}<\left(200-x_{2}\right) \cdot x_{2}<\cdots<\left(200-x_{k}\right) \cdot x_{k}$. So all numbers in these pairs are different and greater than 100. So at most one from each pair is in the set $X$. Therefore, there are at least $k$ numbers greater than 100 and $99-k$ numbers less than 100 that are not in the set $X$, together at least 99 numbers out of 10000 not being in the set $X$.

problem: 1. Solve the inequality $\lg \left(5^{x}+x-20\right)>x-x \lg 2$.
solution:
Solution. Since

$$
x-x \lg 2=x(\lg 10-\lg 2)=x \lg 5=\lg 5^{x}
$$

The inequality takes the form

$$
\lg \left(5^{x}+x-20\right)>\lg 5^{x}
$$

From this

$$
5^{x}+x-20>0,5^{x}+x-20>5^{x}, \text{ so } x>20
$$

problem: 3. What is the remainder when the number $1+2+2^{2}+2^{3}+\ldots+2^{2021}$ is divided by 9?
solution:
First method:

The number 1 when divided by 9 gives a remainder of 1.

The number 2 when divided by 9 gives a remainder of 2.

The number $2^{2}$ when divided by 9 gives a remainder of 4.

The number $2^{3}$ when divided by 9 gives a remainder of 8.

The number $2^{4}$ when divided by 9 gives a remainder of 7.

The number $2^{5}$ when divided by 9 gives a remainder of 5.

1 POINT

Since $2^{6}$ gives a remainder of 1 when divided by 9, the remainders of the number $2^{n}$ when divided by 9 repeat periodically with a period of 6.

Therefore, we first calculate the sum of the remainders for the first six addends $1+2+4+8+7+5=27$ and conclude that the sum $1+2+2^{2}+2^{3}+2^{4}+2^{5}$ is divisible by 9.

2 POINTS

Since $2^{6+k}=2^{6} \cdot 2^{k}$, $2^{6+k}$ for any non-negative integer $k$ gives the same remainder when divided by $k$ as $2^{k}$, i.e., since the remainders of the number $2^{n}$ when divided by 9 repeat periodically with a period of 6, we conclude that the sum $2^{6 k}+2^{6 k+1}+2^{6 k+2}+2^{6 k+3}+2^{6 k+4}+2^{6 k+5}$ is divisible by 9 for any non-negative integer $k$. 3 POINTS

The sum $1+2+2^{2}+2^{3}+\ldots+2^{2021}$ has 2022 addends.

1 POINT

Since 2022 is divisible by 6,

1 POINT the addends in the original sum can be grouped into sets of 6 addends (there are 337 such sets because $2022: 6=337$) whose sum is divisible by 9

1 POINT and thus we conclude that the original sum is divisible by 9, i.e., the remainder when the number $1+2+2^{2}+2^{3}+\ldots+2^{2021}$ is divided by 9 is equal to 0.

1 POINT

Note: Instead of writing generally that each sum $2^{6 k}+2^{6 k+1}+2^{6 k+2}+2^{6 k+3}+2^{6 k+4}+2^{6 k+5}$ for any non-negative integer $k$ is divisible by 9, the student can write that, because the remainders of the number $2^{n}$ when divided by 9 repeat periodically with a period of 6, each of the sums $1+2+2^{2}+2^{3}+2^{4}+2^{5}$, $2^{6}+2^{7}+2^{8}+2^{9}+2^{10}+2^{11}$, $2^{12}+2^{13}+2^{14}+2^{15}+2^{16}+2^{17}$, etc., is divisible by 9.

Two tangent lines $P A$ and $P B$ are drawn from point $P$ to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9$, with the points of tangency being $A$ and $B$. The line $A B$ intersects the $x$-axis and $y$-axis at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. Then the minimum value of the area of $\triangle O M N$ is $\qquad$
solution:

problem:
Z1) Let $n \geq 2$ be a natural number. Let $d_{1}, \ldots, d_{r}$ be all distinct positive divisors of $n$ that are smaller than $n$ itself. Determine all $n$ for which applies:

$$
\operatorname{kgV}\left(d_{1}, \ldots, d_{r}\right) \neq n
$$

Note: For $n=18$, for example, you would have $d_{1}=1, d_{2}=2, d_{3}=3, d_{4}=6, d_{5}=9$ and therefore $\operatorname{kgV}(1,2,3,6,9)=18$.
solution:
Solution (Viviane): If $n$ is a prime power, $n=p^{\alpha}$ applies to a prime number $p$. The divisors of $n$ smaller than $n$ are then $d_{1}=1, d_{2}=p, \ldots, d_{r}=p^{\alpha-1}$. Thus, $k g V\left(1, p, \ldots, p^{\alpha-1}\right)=p^{\alpha-1} \neq n$.

If $n$ is not a prime power, then $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ for a $k \geq 2$. Then $n$ has the two real divisors $p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}$ and $p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$. Furthermore, $k g V\left(d_{1}, \ldots, d_{r}\right) \geq k g V\left(p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}, p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}\right)=n$. Since all $d_{i}$ are divisors of $n$, $k g V\left(d_{1}, \ldots, d_{r}\right) \mid n$ also applies and therefore $\operatorname{kgV}\left(d_{1}, \ldots, d_{r}\right)=n$ must apply.

This means that the $n$ you are looking for are exactly the prime powers.

In a non-isosceles triangle $ABC$, the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$ are inversely proportional to the opposite sides. Find angle $C$.
solution:
Let $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ be the angle bisectors of the triangle, and $A A_{2}, B B_{2}$ be its altitudes. By the given condition, $A A_{1}: A A_{2}=B B_{1}: B B_{2}$, and thus, $\angle A_{1} A A_{2}=\angle B_{1} B B_{2}$. But

$\angle A_{1} A A_{2}=|\angle B-\angle C|, \angle B_{1} B B_{2}=|\angle A-\angle C|$. Since the triangle is not isosceles, the equality $\angle A-\angle C=$ $\angle B-\angle C$ is impossible. Therefore,

$\angle C=1 / 2(\angle A+\angle B)=60^{\circ}$.

## Answer

$60^{\circ}$.

problem:
Do there exist irrational numbers a and b such that the power a ${}^{b}$ is a rational number?

#
solution:
As a, we can take the square root of a natural number.

## Solution

First solution. An example can be the numbers a $=10^{1 / 2}, \mathrm{~b}=2 \lg 11$. Indeed, $\mathrm{a}^{\mathrm{b}}=\left(10^{1 / 2}\right)^{2 \lg 11}=10^{(1 / 2) * 2 \lg 11}=$ $10^{\lg 11}=11$. It remains to show that the numbers $10^{1 / 2}$ and $\lg 11$ are irrational. If it were true that $10^{1 / 2}=\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{n}$ for some natural numbers $\mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{n}$, then the equation $10 \mathrm{n}^{2}=\mathrm{m}^{2}$ would hold, which is impossible since the prime factor 2 enters the left side to an odd power and the right side to an even power. If it were true that $\lg 11=\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{n}$ for some natural numbers $\mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{n}$, then the equation $10^{\mathrm{m}}=11^{\mathrm{n}}$ would hold, which is obviously impossible.

Second solution. Consider the number $A=\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$. If it is rational, the problem is solved (the number $\sqrt{2}$, as is known, is irrational). If $A$ is irrational, then the number $A^{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}^{2}=2$ is rational, so $A$ and $\sqrt{2}$ are the desired numbers.

## Answer

they exist.

problem: The given points of tangency of the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ on the sides are $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$. The sides, angles, and area of $\triangle A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ need to be calculated!
solution:
$1^{0}$. Let $I$ be the center of the inscribed circle of $\triangle ABC$. The angle $\angle B_{1}IC_{1}=180^{\circ}-\alpha$. Let the radius of the inscribed circle of $\triangle ABC$ be $r$. The triangle $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$; therefore,

$$
B_{1}C_{1}=2r \sin \frac{1}{2}(180^{\circ}-\alpha)=2r \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{2t}{s} \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}
$$

Here, $t$ represents the area of $\triangle ABC$, and $s$ represents half the perimeter of $\triangle ABC$. Similarly,

$$
C_{1}A_{1}=\frac{2t}{s} \cos \frac{\beta}{2}, \quad A_{1}B_{1}=\frac{2t}{s} \cos \frac{\gamma}{2}
$$

$2^{0}$. The angles of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ are inscribed angles in a circle of radius $r$. The inscribed angle $\alpha_{1}=\angle B_{1}A_{1}C_{1}$ corresponds to the central angle $\angle B_{1}IC_{1}=180^{\circ}-\alpha$. Therefore,

$$
\alpha_{1}=90^{\circ}-\frac{\alpha}{2}, \quad \beta_{1}=90^{\circ}-\frac{\beta}{2}, \quad \gamma_{1}=90^{\circ}-\frac{\gamma}{2}
$$

$3^{0}$. Let $t_{1}$ be the area of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$. The radius of its circumscribed circle is $r$, so

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{1}=\frac{a_{1}b_{1}c_{1}}{4r}=\frac{(2r)^{3}}{4r} \cos \frac{\alpha}{2} \cos \frac{\beta}{2} \cos \frac{\gamma}{2}=2r^{2} \sqrt{\frac{s(s-a)}{bc}} \sqrt{\frac{s(s-b)}{ca}} \sqrt{\frac{s(s-c)}{ab}}= \\
=\frac{2r^{2}}{abc} s \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}=\frac{2r^{2}}{4Rt} \cdot s \cdot t=\frac{2r \cdot(rs)t}{4Rt} \\
t_{1}=\frac{r}{2R} t
\end{gathered}
$$

Here, $t$ represents the area of $\triangle ABC$, and $R$ represents the radius of its circumscribed circle.

problem:
Given 10 numbers - one one and nine zeros. It is allowed to choose two numbers and replace each of them with their arithmetic mean.

What is the smallest number that can end up in the place of the one?

#
solution:
We will prove by induction on $k$ the following statement: if at some moment there are exactly $k$ non-zero numbers, then each of these numbers is not less than $2^{1-k}$.

Base. For $k=1$, this is true, since after the first non-trivial operation, at least two non-zero numbers will appear, and the number of non-zero numbers will not decrease thereafter.

Inductive Step. Suppose at some moment there are $k+1$ non-zero numbers. Consider the sequence of operations that resulted in these numbers. In this sequence of operations, find the last moment when there were exactly $k$ non-zero numbers. By the inductive hypothesis, each of these numbers is not less than $2^{1-k}$. In the next operation, one zero and one non-zero number were replaced by their average. After this, each of these numbers became not less than $2^{-k}$. In subsequent operations involving only non-zero numbers, the minimum of non-zero numbers does not decrease.

Since we have a total of 10 numbers, each of them is not less than $2^{-9}=1 / 512$.

On the other hand, it is not difficult to provide an example of operations that result in $1 / 512$ from a unit. Replace the unit and one of the zeros with $1 / 2$ and $1 / 2$, then replace $1 / 2$ and another zero with $1 / 4$ and $1 / 4$, and so on; in the end, we get $1 / 512$ from the unit.

## Answer

$1 / 512$.

problem:
1.48 In the expression $x_{1}: x_{2}: \cdots: x_{n}$, use parentheses to indicate the order of operations, and the result can be written in fractional form:
$$
\frac{x_{i_{1}} x_{i_{2}} \cdots x_{i_{k}}}{x_{j_{1}} x_{j_{2}} \cdots x_{j_{n-k}}}
$$
(At the same time, each letter in $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}$ may appear in the numerator or in the denominator.) How many different fractions can be obtained by adding parentheses in all possible ways?
solution:
[Solution] Clearly, $x_{1}$ will be in the numerator of the resulting fraction.
When parentheses are added arbitrarily, the division sign before $x_{2}$ is either related to $x_{2}$ or to an expression in the numerator that includes $x_{2}$, so $x_{2}$ will always be in the denominator.

We will use induction to prove that each of the remaining $n-2$ letters $x_{3}, x_{4}, \cdots, x_{n}$ can independently be in the numerator or the denominator, thus yielding $2^{n-2}$ fractions in total.
Indeed, when $n=3$, we can get 2 fractions:
$$
\left(x_{1}: x_{2}\right): x_{3}=\frac{x_{1}}{x_{2} x_{3}} \text { and } x_{1}:\left(x_{2}: x_{3}\right)=\frac{x_{1} x_{3}}{x_{2}} .
$$

So the conclusion holds for $n=3$.
Assume the conclusion holds for $n=k$, we will prove it for $n=k+1$.
Suppose that after adding parentheses in some way, the expression $x_{1}: x_{2}: \cdots: x_{k}$ can be written in the form of some fraction $A$. If in this expression we replace $x_{k}$ with $x_{k}: x_{k+1}$, then $x_{k}$ will still be in its original position in $A$, and $x_{k+1}$ will not be in the original position of $x_{k}$, that is, if $x_{k}$ was originally in the denominator, then $x_{k+1}$ will be in the numerator, and vice versa.

On the other hand, after adding parentheses in the fraction $A$, there will certainly be an expression of the form $\left(p: x_{k}\right)$, where $P$ is either the letter $x_{k-1}$ or some parentheses. Replacing $\left(p: x_{k}\right)$ with $\left[\left(P: x_{k}\right): x_{k+1}\right]=P: \left(x_{k} \cdot x_{k+1}\right)$, it is clear that in the original fraction $A$, $x_{k} \cdot x_{k+1}$ replaces $x_{k}$. That is, $x_{k+1}$ can be in the same position as $x_{k}$, either both in the numerator or both in the denominator.

By the principle of mathematical induction, each of the remaining $n-2$ letters can independently be in the numerator or the denominator.
Therefore, by adding parentheses in all possible ways, we can obtain $2^{n-2}$ different fractions.

problem: 1. (17 points) Find the area of the triangle cut off by the line $y=2x+2$ from the figure defined by the inequality $|x-2|+|y-3| \leq 3$.
solution:
Answer: 3.

Solution. The figure defined by the given inequality is a square.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_0785b6f179aec901e215g-3.jpg?height=417&width=486&top_left_y=805&top_left_x=882)

The side of the square is $3 \sqrt{2}$ (this value can be found using the Pythagorean theorem). Therefore, the area of the cut-off right triangle is $S=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot 3 \sqrt{2}=3$ square units.

problem: Problem 2. Find all pairs of integers $(a, b)$ for which $a=\frac{4 b-5}{b-2}$
solution:
Solution. The given expression can be transformed as follows:

$$
a=\frac{4 b-5}{b-2}=\frac{4(b-2)+8-5}{b-2}=\frac{4(b-2)}{b-2}+\frac{3}{b-2}=4+\frac{3}{b-2}
$$

The number $a$ will be an integer if and only if $\frac{3}{b-2}$ is an integer, which is true if and only if $b-2$ is a divisor of 3, i.e., if and only if $b-2 \in\{1,-1,3,-3\}$.

Accordingly, there are four possibilities, namely:

- For $b-2=1$ we get $b=3, a=4+3=7$,
- For $b-2=-1$ we get $b=1, a=4-3=1$,
- For $b-2=3$ we get $b=5, a=4+1=5$ and
- For $b-2=-3$ we get $b=-1, a=4-1=3$.

The required pairs are: $(7,3),(1,1),(5,5)$ and $(3,-1)$.

problem:
Franklin B.P.

From the altitudes of a triangle, a triangle can be formed. Is it true that a triangle can also be formed from its angle bisectors?

#

problem: Example 8 One evening, 21 people made $n$ phone calls to each other. It is known that among them, $m$ ($m$ is an odd number) people $a_{1}, a_{2}$, $\cdots, a_{m}$ made phone calls such that $a_{i}$ and $a_{i+1}\left(i=1,2, \cdots, m ; a_{m+1}=a_{1}\right)$ communicated. If among these 21 people, no three people communicated with each other, find the maximum value of $n$. ${ }^{[4]}$
solution:
【Analysis】Construct a graph theory model to characterize the relationships between elements in the problem. From the conditions given in the problem, we know that there is an odd cycle in the graph. Since the number of points is finite, by the extremal principle, there must be a shortest odd cycle $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{2 k+1} A_{1}$. For any two points $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}(j \neq i \pm 1)$ within the shortest odd cycle, they must not be connected, thus the internal structure of the odd cycle is fully understood. At this point, starting from the shortest odd cycle $C$, the entire graph can be divided into two parts: one part is the odd cycle $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{2 k+1} A_{1}$, and the other part is all the points except $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{2 k+1} A_{1}$. We only need to understand the structure of each part and the connection situation between the two parts to grasp the overall structure.
Solution: Use 21 points to represent 21 people.
If two people communicate by phone, then connect the corresponding two points with an edge; otherwise, do not connect an edge, resulting in a graph $G$. It is known that graph $G$ contains an odd cycle, and there are no triangles in graph $G$, and we need to find the maximum value of the number of edges $n$ in graph $G$.

Assume the length of the shortest odd cycle $C$ in the graph is $2 k+1$.
Since there are no triangles in graph $G$, we have $k \geqslant 2$.
Let $C$ be $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{2 k+1} A_{1}$. Then for any $i, j(1 \leqslant i, j \leqslant 2 k+1)$, $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}(j \neq i \pm 1)$ are not connected $\left(A_{0}=A_{2 k+2}=A_{1}\right)$ (otherwise, there would be a shorter odd cycle, contradicting the assumption). For the remaining
$$
21-(2 k+1)=2(10-k)
$$

points, there are no triangles.
By Turán's theorem, the maximum number of edges among these $2(10-k)$ points is $\frac{1}{4}(20-2 k)^{2}=(10-k)^{2}$. Additionally, each of these $2(10-k)$ points cannot be connected to two adjacent vertices in $C$ (otherwise, there would be a triangle, contradicting the assumption), so each of these $2(10-k)$ points can be connected to at most $k$ vertices in $C$. Therefore, the number of edges $n$ in the graph satisfies
$$
\begin{array}{l}
n \leqslant 2 k+1+(10-k)^{2}+2(10-k) k \\
=102-(k-1)^{2} \leqslant 102-(2-1)^{2}=101 .
\end{array}
$$

Suppose the 21 vertices of $G$ are $A_{1}, A_{2}, \cdots, A_{21}$,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
X=\left\{A_{1}, A_{2}, \cdots, A_{5}\right\}, \\
Y=\left\{A_{6}, A_{8}, A_{10}, \cdots, A_{20}\right\}, \\
Z=\left\{A_{7}, A_{9}, A_{11}, \cdots, A_{21}\right\} .
\end{array}
$$
In $X$, $A_{i}$ is connected to $A_{i+1}(i=1,2,3,4)$ and $A_{5}$ is connected to $A_{1}$, in $Y$ each point is connected to each point in $Z$, each point in $Y$ is connected to two points $A_{1}, A_{3}$ in $X$, and each point in $Z$ is connected to two points $A_{2}, A_{4}$ in $X$, and no other two points are connected. Then the number of edges in graph $G$ is
$$
n=5+8 \times 8+2 \times 8 \times 2=101 \text {, }
$$

and graph $G$ contains an odd cycle $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{5} A_{1}$, but no triangles.
In summary, the maximum value of $n$ is 101.

problem: What are the conditions for two medians of a triangle to be perpendicular to each other?
solution:
Let the medians from vertices $A$ and $B$ of triangle $ABC$ be perpendicular to each other. Thus, from their common point, the centroid $S$, the side $AB$ is seen at a right angle, meaning $S$ lies on the circumference of the Thales circle with diameter $AB$, so the distance from $S$ to the midpoint $C_1$ of side $AB = c$ is equal to half the side: $SC_1 = AB / 2$. And since $S$ trisects the median $C_1C$, it follows that $C_1C = 3AB / 2$, meaning $C$ lies on the circle centered at $C_1$ with radius $s_c = 3c / 2$. - Our reasoning can be reversed, so the condition is not only necessary but also sufficient.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_6b5d67b1113868420ed6g-1.jpg?height=628&width=672&top_left_y=388&top_left_x=716)

The median $CC_1 = s_c$ in any triangle can be simply expressed in terms of the three sides, so the above condition can be transformed into a metric condition involving the sides of the triangle. Let the reflection of $C$ over $C_1$ be $C^*$, then in the parallelogram $CACA^*B$ the relationship between the diagonals and sides is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
CC^{*2} + AB^2 & = AC^2 + CB^2 + BC^{*2} + C^*A^2 \\
4s_c^2 + c^2 & = 2a^2 + 2b^2
\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the condition specializes to $2s_c = 3c$:

$$
5c^2 = a^2 + b^2
$$

and this is also necessary and sufficient for the medians corresponding to sides $a$ and $b$ to be perpendicular in a triangle with sides $a$, $b$, and $c$.

Remark. From the fact that in the examined triangles $C$ lies on the circle centered at $C_1$ with radius $3c / 2 = 3 \cdot AC_1 = 3 \cdot BC_1$, it follows that the other two sides are in magnitude between $c$ and $2c$: $c < a, b < 2c$, because for the points $B'$ and $A'$ on the line $AB$ closest to $A$ and farthest from $A$ respectively, we have $B'A = AB = BA' = c$, $AA' = 2c$, and if $C$ coincided with $B'$ or $A'$, a proper triangle would not be formed.

However, we must also specify that $c$ is the shortest side of the triangle. If, for example, $a = \vartheta c$ where $0 < \vartheta \leq 1$, then from (1):

$$
b^2 = (5 - \vartheta^2)c^2 \geq 4c^2, \quad b \geq 2c
$$

and in this case, a triangle with sides $a$, $b$, and $c$ cannot be constructed because the triangle inequality is not satisfied, as $b \geq a + c$.[^0]

[^0]: The auxiliary theorem used is obtained by applying the Pythagorean theorem to the right triangles $CC^*C_0$, $ABB_0$, $ACC_0$, and $BC^*B_0$, where $B_0$ and $C_0$ are the projections of $B$ and $C$ onto the line $AC^*$.

416. In the circle $x^{2}+y^{2} \leqslant R^{2}$, the two-dimensional probability density is $f(x, y)=C\left(R-\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right)$; outside the circle $f(x, y)=0$. Find: a) the constant $C$; b) the probability that a random point $(X, Y)$ falls into the circle of radius $r=1$ centered at the origin, if $R=2$.
solution:
Solution. a) Using the second property of the two-dimensional probability density:

$$
\iint_{(D)} C\left(R-\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right) \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{~d} y=1
$$

From this,

$$
C=1 / \int_{(D)}\left(R-\sqrt{\left.x^{2}+y^{2}\right)} \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{~d} y\right.
$$

By switching to polar coordinates, we get

$$
C=1 / \int_{0}^{2 \pi} d \varphi \int_{0}^{R}(R-\rho) \rho \mathrm{d} \rho=3 /\left(\pi R^{2}\right)
$$

b) According to the condition, $R=2$; therefore, $C=3 /(8 \pi)$ and

$$
f(x, y)=(3 / 8 \pi)\left(2-\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right)
$$

The probability of a random point $(X, Y)$ falling into a circle of radius $r=1$ centered at the origin (region $D_{1}$)

$$
P\left[(X, Y) \subset D_{1}\right]=(3 / 8 \pi) \iint_{\left(D_{1}\right)}\left(2-\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right) d x d y
$$

By switching to polar coordinates, we finally get the desired probability:

$$
P=(3 / 8 \pi) \int_{0}^{2 \pi} d \varphi \int_{0}^{1}(2-\rho) \rho d \rho=1 / 2
$$

problem:
14-17 Let $n$ be a natural number. How many solutions does the equation $x^{2}-\left[x^{2}\right]=(x-[x])^{2}$ have in the interval $1 \leqslant x \leqslant n$?
(Swedish Mathematical Competition, 1982)
solution:
[Solution] Clearly, $x=n$ is a solution to the equation.
Let $1 \leqslant x<n$.
Denote
$$
\begin{array}{l}
m=[x],\{x\}=\alpha, \text { then } \\
x=m+\alpha, \\
x^{2}=m^{2}+2 m \alpha+\alpha^{2}, \quad 0 \leqslant \alpha<1 .
\end{array}
$$

Substituting into the given equation, we get
$$
\begin{array}{c}
m^{2}+2 m \alpha+\alpha^{2}-\left[m^{2}+2 m \alpha+\alpha^{2}\right]=\alpha^{2}, \\
m^{2}+2 m \alpha-m^{2}-\left[2 m \alpha+\alpha^{2}\right]=0, \\
2 m \alpha-\left[2 m \alpha+\alpha^{2}\right]=0, \\
2 m \alpha=\left[2 m \alpha+\alpha^{2}\right] .
\end{array}
$$

Thus, $2 m \alpha$ is an integer.
To make $2 m \alpha$ an integer, and since $0 \leqslant \alpha<1$, then
$$
\alpha=0, \frac{1}{2 m}, \frac{2}{2 m}, \cdots, \frac{2 m-1}{2 m} .
$$

Therefore, for each fixed $m$, $\alpha$ can take $2 m$ values, i.e., there are $2 m$ solutions.
Since $m$ can take $1,2, \cdots, n-1$, then there are
$$
2[1+2+\cdots+(n-1)]=n(n-1)
$$

solutions, plus the solution $x=n$, then there are
$$
n(n-1)+1=n^{2}-n+1 \text { solutions. }
$$

problem: Problem 3. Vasya wants to find all integers $a$ such that the expression $10 n^{3}-3 n^{5}+7$ is divisible by 15 for all integers $n$. What remainders can the number $a$ give when divided by 15? Provide all possible answers or prove that there are no such integers $a$.
solution:
Answer: 14.

Solution. First, let's show that $n^{3} \equiv n(\bmod 3)$ and $n^{5} \equiv n(\bmod 5)$ for any natural $n$. This can be done in several ways. We will present only three of them.

First method. We will divide all natural numbers into groups based on their remainders when divided by 3 and 5:

| $n$ | $n^{3}$ | $n^{3} \bmod 3$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 8 | 2 |


| $n$ | $n^{5}$ | $n^{5} \bmod 5$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 32 | 2 |
| 3 | 243 | 3 |
| 4 | 1024 | 4 |

From the table, it is clear that the statement to be proved is true.

Second method. Note that $n^{3}-n=(n-1) n(n+1)$ is the product of three consecutive integers, and

$$
n^{5}-n=(n-1) n(n+1)\left(n^{2}+1\right) \equiv(n-1) n(n+1)\left(n^{2}-4\right)=(n-2)(n-1) n(n+1)(n+2) \quad(\bmod 5)
$$

is the product of five consecutive integers. In the first case, the expression is always divisible by 3, and in the second case, by 5, which is what we needed to prove.

The third method is to say that these statements are special cases of Fermat's Little Theorem.

Now let's look at the original expression modulo 3:

$$
10 n^{3}-3 n^{5}+7 a n \equiv 10 n+7 a n \equiv(a+1) \cdot n \quad(\bmod 3)
$$

This expression is divisible by 3 for any integer $n$ if and only if $a+1$ is divisible by 3, i.e., when $a$ gives a remainder of 2 when divided by 3. Similarly, $10 n^{3}-3 n^{5}+7 a n \equiv(2 a+2) \cdot n(\bmod 5)$, i.e., $2 a+2$ is divisible by 5, so $a$ gives a remainder of 4 when divided by 5.

Thus, $a \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$ and $a \equiv 4(\bmod 5)$, i.e., $a \equiv 14(\bmod 15)$.

Another solution. Substitute $n=1$ and we get that if such an $a$ exists, then $7+7 a$ must be divisible by 15, i.e., $a$ must give a remainder of 14 when divided by 15. It remains to check that if $a \equiv 14(\bmod 15)$, then the given expression is divisible by 15 for any natural $n$. This can be done in many ways (see, for example, the first solution). Here we will present another one.

We will prove this statement by induction on $n$ (for $n=0$ the divisibility is obvious, for negative $n$ it is proved similarly or reduced to the case of positive $n$ by replacing $n \rightarrow-n$). If $n=1$, the statement has already been verified. Suppose now that we have already proved that $10 n^{3}-3 n^{5}+7 a n$ is divisible by 15 and we will prove that $10(n+1)^{3}-3(n+1)^{5}+7 a(n+1)$ is also divisible by 15. Let's look at the difference between these two expressions:

$10\left((n+1)^{3}-n^{3}\right)-3\left((n+1)^{5}-n^{5}\right)+7 a((n+1)-n)=10\left(3 n^{2}+3 n+1\right)-3\left(5 n^{4}+10 n^{3}+10 n^{2}+5 n+1\right)+7 a$.

After expanding the brackets, all terms on the right side, except for $10-3+7 a$, are divisible by 15, but $10-3+7 a$ is divisible by 15 since $a \equiv 14(\bmod 15)$.

Natural numbers $x, y, z$ are such that $\operatorname{GCD}(\operatorname{LCM}(x, y), z) \cdot \operatorname{LCM}(\operatorname{GCD}(x, y), z)=1400$.

What is the greatest value that $\operatorname{GCD}(\operatorname{LCM}(x, y), z)$ can take?

solution:
# Answer: 10

## Solution:

Notice that $\operatorname{LCM}(\operatorname{GCD}(x, y), z)$ is divisible by $z$, and $z$ is divisible by $\operatorname{GCD}(\operatorname{LCM}(x, y), z)$, so $\operatorname{LCM}(\operatorname{GCD}(x, y), z)$ is divisible by $\operatorname{GCD}(\operatorname{LCM}(x, y), z)$.

$1400=2^{3} \cdot 5^{2} \cdot 7$ and in the second factor, each prime number appears with an exponent no less than in the first. Therefore, the maximum possible value of $\operatorname{GCD}(\operatorname{LCM}(x, y), z)$ is $2 \cdot 5=10$. This value is achieved when $x=y=10, z=140$.

problem:
Lex has $\$ 2.65$. He has only dimes (worth $\$ 0.10$ each) and quarters (worth $\$ 0.25$ each). If Lex has more quarters than dimes, how many coins does he have in total?
(A) 12
(B) 13
(C) 16
(D) 19
(E) 22
solution:
Lex has 265 cents in total.

Since a quarter is worth 25 cents, the total value in cents of the quarters that Lex has is a multiple of 25 , and so must end in $00,25,50$ or 75 .

Since the remaining part of the 265 cents is made up of dimes only, the remaining part is a multiple of 10 , so ends in a 0 .

Thus, the value of the quarters must end with a 5 , so ends with 25 or 75 .

Since Lex has more quarters than dimes, we start by trying to determine the largest possible number of quarters that he could have.

The largest possible value of his quarters is thus 225 cents, which would be $225 \div 25=9$ quarters, leaving $265-225=40$ cents in dimes, or 4 dimes.

Thus, Lex has $9+4=13$ coins in total.

(The next possible largest value of his quarters is 175 cents, which would come from 7 quarters and so 90 cents in dimes or 9 dimes. This does not satisfy the condition that the number of quarters is larger than the number of dimes.)

ANSWER: (B)

problem: Let's find a three-digit number such that the product of the digits in the tens and units place is equal to the two-digit number formed by the leftmost two digits.
solution:
Let the sought three-digit number be

$$
100 x+10 y+z
$$

then according to the condition

$$
y z=10 x+y
$$

or

$$
y(z-1)=10 x
$$

If the product $y(z-1)$ has one factor even, the other must be 5, because neither factor can be greater than 9, and they cannot both be even or equal to 5 at the same time.

If $y=5, z-1$ is even, that is, $z$ is odd and greater than 1, its only values are:

$$
3, \quad 5, \quad 7, \quad 9
$$

and the corresponding solutions are:

$$
153, \quad 255, \quad 357, \quad 459
$$

If $z-1=5$, that is, $z=6$, then $y$ is even and is one of the following numbers:

$$
2, \quad 4, \quad 6, \quad 8
$$

The other four solutions are therefore:

$$

8.56 In the lower left corner square $a 1$ of the chessboard, there is a rook. With each move, the rook can move 1 square horizontally or vertically. Can the rook visit all 64 squares of the chessboard, and visit the 64 squares exactly $1, 2, \cdots, 64$ times respectively, and finally
(1) return to the original starting square $a 1$?
(2) end the journey in square a2?
(The initial position in square $a 1$ also counts as visiting the square 1 time.)
solution:
［Solution］(1) It is impossible to return to the original starting square $a1$. If the final move is back to square $a1$, then the route taken by the rook is closed, meaning the number of moves in both the horizontal and vertical directions are even, so the total number of moves is even.

On the other hand, according to the given information, the total number of times the rook reaches each square on the board is
$$
1+2+\cdots+64=2080
$$

which is even. However, at the start, the rook is already on square $a1$ once, so it needs to move another 2079 times, which is odd, leading to a contradiction.
(2) The journey can end on square $a2$. Number the 64 squares on the board as $1,2, \cdots, 64$ as shown in the figure. When the rook starts from the $k$-th square and sequentially visits squares $k+1, k+2, \cdots, m-1$, and finally reaches the $m$-th square, we denote this route as $k \rightarrow m$. The return route is denoted as $m \rightarrow k$. Consider the following route:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
1 \longrightarrow 64 \rightarrow 1 \rightarrow 63 \rightarrow 2 \longrightarrow 62 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 61 \rightarrow 4 \\
\cdots \rightarrow 30 \rightarrow 34 \rightarrow 31 \longrightarrow 33 \longrightarrow 32 .
\end{array}
$$

It is not difficult to verify that for the $k$-th square satisfying $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 32$, the rook visits it $2k$ times; for the $m$-th square satisfying $33 \leqslant m \leqslant 64$, the rook visits it $129-2m$ times. Additionally, the final square the rook reaches, the 32nd square, is precisely $a2$. This shows that this route meets all the requirements of the problem.

problem:
Berlov S.L.

100 people came to a party. Then those who had no acquaintances among the attendees left. Then those who had exactly one acquaintance among the remaining people also left. Then, similarly, those who had exactly 2, 3, 4, ..., 99 acquaintances among the remaining people at the time of their departure also left.

What is the maximum number of people that could remain at the end?
solution:
It is not difficult to check that if all the attendees, except for two people $A$ and $B$, were acquainted with each other, then at the end, everyone except $A$ and $B$ should have remained, that is, 98 people.

Let's prove that 99 people could not have remained. It is clear that person $A$, who initially had the fewest acquaintances ($k$), would leave at some point. If no one else left, then all the others (except $A$) had more than $k$ acquaintances before $A$ left and fewer than $k+1$ after $A$ left. But then $A$ must have been acquainted with everyone else, meaning $k=99$, which contradicts the strict minimality of $k$.

## Answer

98 people.

problem: If $a+b=2$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}=2$, what is the value of $a^{3}+b^{3}$? And $a^{4}+b^{4}$?
solution: According to the identity above, we have $a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)\left(a^{2}-a b+b^{2}\right)=$ $2(2-a b)$. Therefore, it is sufficient to evaluate $a b$. We have $4=(a+b)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+2 a b=2+2 a b$, hence $a b=1$, and $a^{3}+b^{3}=2$. Next, $4=\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)^{2}=a^{4}+b^{4}+2 a^{2} b^{2}=a^{4}+b^{4}+2$, hence $a^{4}+b^{4}=2$.

problem: There are 1991 participants in a sports event. Each of them knows at least $n$ other participants (the relationship of knowing each other is reciprocal). What is the minimum value of $n$ for which there must necessarily exist a group of 6 participants who know each other pairwise?
solution: We construct a graph where the vertices are the participants, connected by an edge when they know each other. Then every vertex has a degree of at least $n$, and we seek the minimal value of $n$ for which this graph necessarily contains $K_{6}$. According to Zarankiewicz's lemma, a 6-free graph with 1991 vertices contains at least one vertex with a degree less than or equal to $\tilde{\mathrm{A}}\left\lfloor\frac{4 \times 1991}{5}\right\rfloor=1592$. Therefore, the bound $n \geq 1593$ is sufficient. On the other hand, this bound is optimal if we consider the 6-free Turán graph $T(1991,5)$. This graph is the complete 5-partite graph with 399 edges in one of the parts and 398 in the others. The minimal degree of a vertex in this graph is consequently $1991-399=1592$.
